speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the Minister of Finance. Given the fact that the dollar is dropping in the foreign exchange markets, and every one dollar drop causes the rate of inflation to rise four-tenths of 1 per cent over two years, how does the minister plan to start getting the inflation rate in this country down, as long as the devaluation of our dollar continues?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
subtopic: STEPS BY GOVERNMENT TO REDUCE RATE OF INFLATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we have shown what we are planning to do in that field. We had a conference last week on the fiscal, monetary and economic policies of the government. subtopic: STEPS BY GOVERNMENT TO REDUCE RATE OF INFLATION
speechtext: It must be apparent to everyone, and certainly to the Minister of Finance, that the continued devaluation of the Canadian dollar is having an enormous impact on the inflationary rate in this nation. As long as this continues, and as long as the government is not prepared to change the framework within which the value of the dollar is set in international exchanges, we will have more inflation. It makes no sense for the minister to talk about a declining inflation rate unless he is prepared to do something about the external value of the dollar. Is something going to be done about this problem, or shall we have to count on more inflation during the next six months?

NORTHERN PIPELINE-CANADIAN CONTENT AND EFFECT ON CANADIAN JOBS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 have a question for the Deputy Prime Minister. The National Energy Board, in its decision today, has recommended the use of low-pressure pipe for the Alcan route. The only significant benefit to Canada in the Alcan pipeline project is jobs that may occur in this country. It is in this context I would like to ask my question.
Is the Deputy Prime Minister aware that an American government interdepartmental study estimates that approximately 30 per cent of the pipeline, with regard to durable equipment for the Canadian section, will be produced in the United States? That is not from the Wall Street Journal; it is from an American intergovernmental study. Is he aware of that? If so, how does he square it with his assurance to the people of Canada that 90 per cent of such products will be made in Canada?
February 20, 1978

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: NORTHERN PIPELINE-CANADIAN CONTENT AND EFFECT ON CANADIAN JOBS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member knows, no decision on pipe size can be made by the National Energy Board until Bill C-25 is enacted. However, in the report of the National Energy Board which I shall table at three o'clock, the board states its intention, subsequent to the enactment of the legislation, to include within its specifications for the pipeline approval of 56-inch, low-pressure pipe.
It should be borne in mind that this particular pipe size can be manufactured both in Hamilton and Regina and is not presently manufactured in any plant in the United States. That ought to be of some assistance to the hon. member in realizing that the high Canadian content which I have predicted will be possible and will be achievable, notwithstanding the interdepartmental report to which he has referred but which I have not seen. I prefer to rely on statistics given in Canada, rather than those from the United States.

subtopic: NORTHERN PIPELINE-CANADIAN CONTENT AND EFFECT ON CANADIAN JOBS
speechtext: I find it an extraordinary admission from the minister, who was in charge of negotiations for Canada, that he has not seen the report. I have a copy of it right here and would be glad to send it over to him. I repeat, Mr. Speaker, it is an American government interdepartmental study which estimates they are going to get 67 per cent, up to two-thirds, of the business-if not more-in the United States. The minister has not seen that report. I also have here the study done by our Department of Regional Economic Expansion, which reaches precisely the same conclusion as the American study.

subtopic: NORTHERN PIPELINE-CANADIAN CONTENT AND EFFECT ON CANADIAN JOBS
speechtext: Oh!

subtopic: NORTHERN PIPELINE-CANADIAN CONTENT AND EFFECT ON CANADIAN JOBS
speechtext:
The Canadian study says, on page 9:
Unless there is effective control ensuring Canadian content, 67 per cent may be a more realistic projection.
In other words, the Canadian study agrees with the findings of the American study that without guarantees the minister's promise to the Canadian people is hogwash. How does the hon. gentleman account for this?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: NORTHERN PIPELINE-CANADIAN CONTENT AND EFFECT ON CANADIAN JOBS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there are two points one must make in reply to the hon. gentleman's question. The first is that the Department of Regional Economic Expansion developed a "worst possible" scenario. This indicated the vulnerabilities to which Canadian competition might be exposed. It seems to me it was very wise for the department to make that kind of "worst case" scenario in order that it could be avoided. The hon. member quotes from the report as saying that unless effective control or effective monitoring-

subtopic: NORTHERN PIPELINE-CANADIAN CONTENT AND EFFECT ON CANADIAN JOBS
speechtext: Control.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: NORTHERN PIPELINE-CANADIAN CONTENT AND EFFECT ON CANADIAN JOBS
speechtext:
All right, effective control. He says unless effective control is possible, then 67 per cent might be the worst possible result. I want to assure the hon. member that when he reads the bill presently before the House, he will realize there is a provision in the legislation giving the agency,
Oral Questions
and finally the minister, a very obvious way of maintaining effective control over Canadian content. Certainly, I would not bring a bill before the House of Commons and ask that it be passed unless there were to be effective control by the agency and the government over the Canadian content provisions.

subtopic: NORTHERN PIPELINE-CANADIAN CONTENT AND EFFECT ON CANADIAN JOBS
speechtext:
My final supplementary, Mr. Speaker, is this. The minister has misinformed the House about the DREE report. The DREE report refers to the minister's estimate of 90 per cent content as being wishful thinking. It is the minister who has taken the most optimistic forecast of possibilities and has made a promise to Canadians. The DREE report, produced by his own government, said it would be more like 67 per cent, and that this was not a "doomsday" forecast; it was a more realistic projection. So the minister has quite categorically misinformed the House about what this report says.
By way of a final question to the minister, having had some discussions with leaders of the steel industry in Canada, is he aware of the fact that our steel industry is not concerned about competition from the U.S. steel industry, but is very much concerned about the Japanese steel industry which produced the pipe for Alaska, and about the Italian and German steel industries which produced the pipe for the Soviet Union?

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PREVENT DUMPING OF STEEL BEAMS- DEFINITION OF "FAIR WORLD PRICE"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Finance. The temporary hoist, under section 17 of the Financial Administration Act, of the 30 per cent dumping duty on wide-flange steel beams gives needed and just relief to steel fabricators working on fixed-price contracts. However, as the minister must know, it does absolutely nothing to resolve the present and future injury to the economies of British Columbia and Newfoundland, and it does nothing to remove the uncertainty facing some 1,000 to 2,000 steelworkers jobs in British Columbia.
Can the minister help clear the uncertainty that clouds the B.C. scene by advising whether, in using the f.o.b. Portland price as the definition of "fair world price", that f.o.b. Portland price will be free and clear of any effect the U.S. trigger price formula might have on it for Canadian purposes?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: MEASURES TO PREVENT DUMPING OF STEEL BEAMS- DEFINITION OF "FAIR WORLD PRICE"
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we said in our statement that we have to remit a dumping duty to give relief in that field until June 29, because we have to go by the decision of the Anti-dumping Tribunal which established that this type of steel was being dumped on the Canadian market. speakeroldname: Hon. Alastair Gillespie (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):

subtopic: GLACE BAY, N.S.-SUGGESTED DISCRIMINATION IN AECL PAYMENTS IN LIEU OF TAXES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there is no discrimination. Mr. Speaker, before resuming my comments on this bill I should like to thank the minister and his officials for providing me with the guidelines which had not been distributed-and I underline they had not been distributed-prior to the beginning of this debate though, according to the date I have here they were issued in December, 1977. They ought to have been available to all members participating in the debate, but I found them on my desk when I returned to my office after speaking last Wednesday. It is a deferred acknowledgment and I am sorry it had to be this way, but we now have the guidelines and I think they are very important.
When I called it six o'clock on Wednesday evening I had reached the point of examining the provisions of the bill that will permit more extensive inquiries into the environmental impacts that are likely to occur and the inquiries that will be carried on under the provisions of the bill that were mentioned
Northern Pipeline
either in the Lysyk inquiry or in the environmental assessment and review panel study.
I think it ought to be mentioned as a general comment about the Alaska Highway part of the pipeline that there has been reference to the need to take permafrost into account. Those who have not been in the Yukon may not be aware that the permafrost problem does not apply all the way along the Alaska Highway. It is the Dempster cut-off that would have the problems of permafrost.
I think it should be said, however, that perhaps partly because of the short time available to Dean Lysyk to prepare his report, he devoted little space to the environmental problems likely to arise, whereas the Berger inquiry, which had more time at its disposal, covered environmental problems more fully. The other reason the Lysyk inquiry did not deal with environmental issues was that its terms of reference provided for representation from the environmental assessment and review panel which allowed those elements to be taken into account. It may have been that Dean Lysyk felt that the strictly environmental problems could be left to be dealt with by the panel.
I feel it is necessary to point out that one of the principal differences between the Lysyk and the Berger inquiries is that the Berger inquiry covered all aspects of the matter, while there is no reference whatsoever in the Lysyk inquiry, or by the panel, to British Columbia or Alberta. The Lysyk report dealt solely with the Yukon. I think this oversight will have to be taken into account. Fortunately, a clause in Schedule III of the bill requires that the pipeline company carry out the necessary studies into fisheries, environmental and socio-economic problems.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to take part in this historic debate dealing with one of the largest undertakings ever addressed by a group from the private sector. In many ways I think it is not only an historic debate but an historic project in the development of our country-to link the third sea, the Arctic Sea, to the Atlantic Ocean; indeed, perhaps of linking the Arctic Sea to the Atlantic Ocean. I will have more to say about that in my remarks to follow.
In the time available to me I shall attempt to deal with three areas, first of all the size of the pipe, secondly the need for Canada to gain access to Canadian natural gas resources in the Mackenzie Delta area, and thirdly I will talk about the attractiveness of the option which has been opened up for
3014

February 20, 1978
Northern Pipeline
Canada as a result of the pipeline treaty negotiated with the United States.
The President of Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) has already tabled the report of the National Energy Board dealing with the question of what should be the appropriate size of pipe for the section of the line from Whitehorse to Caroline. There may have been some surprise that the stated position of the National Energy Board came down in favour of the 56-inch option rather than the one which has received a good deal of attention in the press, that is to say, the 54-inch option and the option included in the pipeline treaty with the United States.
I would like to take a few moments to deal with the question of the 56-inch pipe. Its origin comes from the initiative of United States officials during the December meeting of the technical committee which addressed itself to these questions. At that time the suggestion was made that a 56-inch pipe at 1,080 psi should be considered as an alternative to the 54-inch pipe at 1,120 psi because there was more world experience in manufacturing and installing 56-inch diameter pipe than in the 54-inch diameter pipe. While at the time Canada and United States negotiations were continuing, 54-inch diameter pipe had been shown as the appropriate larger diameter pipe for consideration, Foothills agreed that it would have been just as logical to have selected the 56-inch diameter pipe in relation to the 3.6 billion cubic feet a day of gas anticipated as the throughput.
The United States response included the consideration of the use of 56-inch diameter pipe as one alternative. This has been taken into account in the Board's analysis. I understand that it was concluded in the U.S. reply that any of the systems under consideration, high pressure or low pressure, could be built and operated with equal safety and reliability. It is the view of the National Energy Board, however, that selection of the 48-inch high pressure system, because of the extensive new technology involved and the lack of experience in its use, would present risks.
The Board states in its report that safety and reliability are matters of primary concern to it. There has been a good record in the Canadian pipeline industry in this regard. Also there has been steady improvement in standards related to quality of steel, manufacturing procedures, pipe welding and other construction procedures.
The Board believes that moving from the general operating pressure of 1,000 psi, which is the present practice in North America, to that proposed of the 48-inch 1,680 psi system represents a large step in new technology. The Board would require thorough testing of the 48-inch 0.72 inch wall thickness before approving that design. Foothills has estimated there could be a delay of up to two years in completion of the pipeline in order to carry out such testing before ordering the pipe. This would not be in the interests of the United States or of Canada. On the other hand the board is prepared to approve the use of .54 inch wall thickness pipe of the specifications proposed by Foothills, in 48-inch, 54-inch or 56-inch diameter pipe subject only to confirmatory burst testing prior to com-

mencement of construction. From a design point of view this means there would be no delay in ordering pipe and that planning for all other aspects of the pipeline construction could proceed.
As has been pointed out on many occasions in the House, Mr. Speaker, another important feature in the selection of the .54 inch wall thickness pipe is the fact that two Canadian pipe mills could supply pipe of the quality required and in diameters up to 56 inches. In the case of the heavier wall pipe only one Canadian mill has the manufacturing capabilities, thus reducing reliability and possibly affecting Canadian content. The Board has concluded that from a safety and reliability point of view the final choice of pipe to the pressure range achievable with .54 inch wall thickness, that is to say the 48-inch diameter pipe, the 56-inch diameter pipe and 54-inch diameter pipe should be chosen on the basis of economics. I should add that the 48-inch low pressure pipe should not be considered an option because the pipeline itself, that is the Dempster connection, will be needed before 1990.
The United States response indicated, as I have already stated, that based on the design volumes of 2.4 billion cubic feet a day from Prudhoe Bay, and 1.2 billion cubic feet a day from the Mackenzie Delta, its first choice would be the 48-inch high pressure pipe with its second choice being the 56-inch 1,080 psi pipe.
With respect to the choice of pipe, mention should be made here of paragraph 10 in the Canada-United States Agreement. This particular provision allowed for consideration of any combination of pressure and diameter of pipe which would achieve safety and reliability and economic efficiency. Annex III to the Agreement relating to cost allocation contained cost estimates for 48-inch and 54-inch diameter pipe. If 56-inch diameter pipe was chosen it would require an addendum to Annex III to include costs for the 56-inch alternative which had been agreed on by the two parties to the Agreement. It is the understanding of the government that such an addendum would be considered a technical change. This could be accomplished by an exchange of notes following a meeting of Canadian and United States officials to agree upon the appropriate figures to include in the annex. Inasmuch as the Canada-United States Agreement is contained in Bill C-25 as Schedule I, a corresponding amendment would be required in the bill as well. This could be introduced when the bill is considered by the committee.
As was pointed out to the House, Mr. Speaker, on February 13, no decision could be made by the National Energy Board regarding pipe size until Bill C-25 is enacted. However, in its report the board has indicated that subsequent to enactment it intends to include in its approval of pipeline specifications the 56-inch 0.54 inch wall thickness pipe for that portion of the pipeline between Whitehorse and Caroline. That could provide significant economic benefits to the United States in the order of close to $100 million based on the assumption over 20 years with the choice of 56-inch pipe over 54-inch. Taking the value of the gas at $1.60 mef and assuming an additional throughput
February 20, 1978

of 65 billion cubic feet, there would be a saving to the United States consumer of roughly $100 million.
There would be a comparable saving to the Canadian consumer, again assuming the same time period, but assuming that the gas is not made available until five years later than it becomes available in the United States, using the same figure per 1,000 cubic feet and an additional throughput of 25 billion feet, a saving of $40 million. In summary, economics favour the 56-inch over the 54-inch diameter pipe, with potential savings collectively of $140 million.
I would now like to move to the part of my remarks dealing with the questions of, first, the need for the pipeline and of access and, second, the full question of cost and benefits to Canadians. There have been a number of suggestions to the effect that the Alaska Highway pipeline will do nothing for the Canadian energy situation, that it is designed solely for the United States. It has also been suggested that Canada has no need for the frontier gas, that we already have enough gas in Alberta. I believe that both of those statements are false. I wish to review some of the reasons for believing that to be so.
The bill before the House is designed to give effect to the Canada-United States Agreement. I am sure hon. members are aware this agreement was reached after many, many hours of negotiation with our neighbours to the south. One of the most important issues in those negotiations, perhaps the one most difficult to resolve, was the terms under which Mackenzie Delta gas would be connected into the Alaska Highway pipeline system. The problem is that Canadian gas from the Mackenzie would be expensive. For example, it would be more expensive than gas which is available in the southern basin, although less expensive than gas from the High Arctic and some other alternate energy sources in Canada.
The objective of the Canadian negotiators was to ensure that Canada could obtain access to Delta gas at costs that were not prohibitively high. The Canadian team was able to strike a very good bargain for us in this regard.
The present bill assures Canada the cheapest possible access to our own Delta reserves. It provides that U.S.A. consumers will pay the full cost of shipping the Canadian gas from Dawson to Whitehorse if the Canadian section of the line through the Yukon comes within 35 per cent of the estimated cost of that line and will pay not less than two thirds of the total cost of building that spur from Whitehorse to Dawson if the escalation is greater than the amount 1 just mentioned. The exact share will depend on the final cost of the completed pipeline. In any event, Canadians will be able to get Mackenzie gas in Canadian markets transported from the Mackenzie Delta to southern gas markets at a lower cost than Americans would be able to get American Alaska gas transported from Prudhoe Bay to their markets. That is clearly a significant benefit to Canada.
The existence of the Alcan pipeline, the Foothills (Yukon) pipeline, is the only way at the present time of ensuring access to presently proven reserves in the Delta. These reserves will
Northern Pipeline
provide a significant addition to Canada's proven accessible reserves, but they are simply not large enough to justify a Canadian pipeline at the present time.
My first point then is that this legislation assures Canadians of access to our own Delta gas. Without the pipeline, there is no such assurance. It also assures us we will get that gas at a lower cost than the Americans will get their Alaska gas in the United States. It assures us the lowest possible cost. These benefits clearly are not insignificant. Hon. members who suggest this pipeline does nothing for Canada's energy needs are simply misrepresenting the facts.
I now wish to turn to my second point. Many people are saying that access to gas in the Mackenzie is of dubious value, that we have as much as we possibly need in Alberta and this will look after us until at least the 1990's. There are a number of basic flaws in that argument. There are three basic flaws I want to attack.
The first flaw is that that argument confuses short-term deliverability surplus with long-term reserve availability. Second, that argument ignores the large extent to which natural gas could reduce our reliance on imported oil, is assured long-term supplies of gas were not available. This is a very important point. The third flaw in that argument is that it ignores, by implication, the gravity of the world oil supply problem. I will deal very briefly with the latter point first, the gravity of the world oil supply problem.
A few statistics might place this problem in context because Canada is very much involved in the international oil context. The western world is now consuming about 50 million barrels of oil every day, about 18 billion barrels in the course of the year. Second, the largest oil accumulation ever discovered in North America, that is to say at Prudhoe Bay, ten billion barrels of oil, works out to not much more than six months' supply in terms of the world's consumption at current consumption rates.
The North Sea accumulation was roughly 23 billion barrels. In terms of world supply at current consumption rates, this would add another year and a half. Taking these two very significant discoveries together, they add no more than two years to world supplies at current consumption rates.
All discoveries in the last 15 years, those in North Africa, West Africa, the North Slope, and the North Sea, amount to about 100 billion barrels. That is no more than six years' supply at current consumption rates. Perhaps I have said enough to indicate the horrendous dimension of the oil supply problem in the western world.
More often than not, we are using more oil than we are discovering. More often than not, at the end of the year there is less oil available than there was at the beginning of the year. At the same time, at the end of the year we are consuming more than we were at the beginning of the year. Quite clearly this will lead the western world to an oil crunch, and that crunch may not be far away. Estimates indicate it could occur about 1985, give or take a year or two.

Also, new oil discoveries are proving more expensive. Accumulations are smaller. Canada is no exception to this general rule. Current projections indicate a continuing decline in production from conventional sources over the next ten years, which means increasing reliance on costly unconventional sources such as the tar sands. All this has to be seen against the background of the western world's massive consumption of oil, its apparent inability to decrease its demand, and the reluctance of oil-rich countries in Arabia to increase supplies.
This situation leads inexorably to one conclusion: our dependence upon oil supplies from the Middle East must be reduced. I need hardly remind hon. members of the instability of the area-the tragic events in Cyprus over the week end are, in themselves, an illustration. Take the situation affecting the Horn of Africa, a confrontation between two nations on the edge of the Red Sea right opposite Saudi Arabia. This is yet another reminder of the vulnerability of oil supplies from the Middle East. Saudi Arabia is presently pumping about nine million barrels of oil a day. The best estimate 1 have seen is that it would be required to produce between nine million and 16 million bairels by 1985. Then there is a big jump from 1985 to 1990, a jump which could take the requirement to 23 million or even to 35 million barrels a day.
On the basis of nine million barrels a day, Saudi Arabia is presently generating something like $50 billion a year in foreign exchange. Figures like these stretch the imagination and there is no point spending much time on them except to make the fairly obvious comment: why would a small country of some six million people, which cannot even use the foreign exchange it is generating from oil sales today, want to increase its production significantly in the future? Why would not the leaders of that small country say to themselves, "We would much prefer to keep this important resource in the ground, under our own control rather than exchange it for bank accounts in foreign banks which we do not control." Much of the current debate on the world oil situation focuses on questions of this kind.
Will Saudi Arabia produce at the levels required to meet rising international oil demand? Quite simply, we do not know. But I do not believe Canada and the rest of the western world can afford to take a chance. We have to look to ourselves in order to protect our interests. We have done this collectively through the International Energy Agency and we have set an import target of no more than 26 million barrels a day by 1985. Canada has participated in agreeing to this collective target.
We in Canada have set ourselves an import target of one third of our consumption, or 800,000 barrels a day, whichever is the lesser. That goal will not be easy to reach. We are already net importers of some 200,000 barrels a day. Between 1980 and 1985, Canadian conventional oil production is expected to fall off quickly, perhaps by 500,000 barrels per day. And, inevitably, demand will continue to increase. To reach our import target we shall have to move on several fronts.
Hon. members will be familiar with the three basic principles of Canada's energy policy. First is conservation. We have to accelerate our efforts to conserve and develop renewable energy supplies. Second, we have to develop new, indigenous supplies of oil from sources such as the tar sands. Third, we must direct increasingly more attention to energy substitution. This latter process will involve massive sums of money; many of these projects were identified last week at the first ministers' conference. Natural gas offers the greatest possibility at the present time of decreasing our present dependence on foreign oil. Let me give the House some indication of the way in which this might work.
There is a wide variation across Canada in terms of total energy consumed from oil by the various regions. For example, Albertans consume only about 30 per cent of their total primary energy in the form of oil. But as we move further east, dependence upon oil increases. In Quebec, close to 70 per cent of the primary energy consumed by the population is in the form of oil, and further east still, in the Atlantic provinces, between 80 per cent and 90 per cent is consumed in the form of oil. Roughly two-thirds of that oil is foreign oil. In other words, the region east of Ontario is most vulnerable to any cessation of that foreign oil supply. This does not exclude Ontario because, as conventional sources become depleted, Ontario too could be affected. That pipeline, which was built to be reversible, may yet be used as such. All of which means that the centre of the country would be more dependent on foreign oil than in the past.
Natural gas is one of our great opportunities to reduce dependence on imported oil. By moving natural gas, whether from the Mackenzie Delta or Alberta or the High Arctic into eastern Canada by means of the pipeline presently under consideration, as well as by others which may be built, such as a Quebec and maritimes pipeline, a project which the first ministers endorsed for early application at their meeting last week, a pipeline could carry gas from the Mackenzie all the way to Halifax, a pipeline which could be reversed so that if significant finds of natural gas were proved off Sable Island or off the Labrador shore-

speechtext:
-liquefied natural gas from the High Arctic could be brought into Canso, or Lorneterm at Saint John, for instance, and that gas could be moved back, and the pipeline would be forging a new band of steel across the country. But before this can happen there has to be an assurance of supply. A bubble is not enough. That is why this bill addresses itself to the most important aspect which we are considering, the reduction of our reliance on imported oil.
But some hon. members might still say: Surely Alberta has all the gas we need; why go up to the Mackenzie? In the report of the National Energy Board tabled today by my colleague, the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen), we find this reference to the pipeline on page seven:

February 20, 1978

While recognizing that there has been continuing exploration success in the western Canadian sedimentary basin since the time of the board's report, it is the board's expectation that a detailed review of gas supply and demand in Canada, which will undoubtedly be undertaken within the next year, will still indicate a need for the Dempster lateral prior to 1990.
The words "prior to 1990" are tied in to the question of the 48-inch low pressure pipe which was raised by certain members of the technical team on the U.S. side. My answer is that we cannot rely solely on Alberta. We have to distinguish between a long term deliverability shortage and a short term deliverability surplus. I should expand on those two particular distinctions.
First, I should like to comment on the long term outlook. Alberta has sufficient long term deliverability to satisfy current levels of Canadian consumption, plus small levels of demand growth, but only until the mid-1980's. Our most recent estimates suggest that with modest increases in the share taken by natural gas, long term deliverability from Alberta will only be sufficient to meet demand until the mid-1980's. With luck, the results of the intense drilling now taking place in Alberta will enable us to extend this date by a few years, but not by much.
Even Alberta's resources are finite. The new discoveries being made there are similar to the oil and gas discoveries being made elsewhere in the world. The pools are smaller; they are harder to find; and recovery is more costly. These facts only serve to confirm the belief that the long term availability of gas is still very much in doubt. This is one of the basic constraints that is at present inhibiting the expansion of gas markets in eastern Canada. It is one of the basic reasons why substitution of natural gas for oil is not taking place at a rate that would be consistent with Canada's long term interests.
This fundamental point is often missed, however, because of the second phenomenon now being experienced in Alberta; a short term deliverability surplus. Alberta could now supply, for a five or six year period, more gas than is required to meet Canadian and current export needs. This is why several proposals have been made to increase gas exports to the U.S. on a swap basis.
This short term deliverability surplus should not obscure the basic facts, however. Canada still does not have enough gas to meet its long term needs, where "need" is here defined so as to include a rapidly increasing market share for natural gas. The current rates of discovery in Alberta are certainly encouraging, and it would indeed be fortunate if large, new accumulations proved up in Canada's western basin. But I do not think we can afford to take such a gamble. We cannot afford to say we are sure that these reserves will be proved up. It is quite clear that we need to develop other gas producing areas in Canada as well, and we have to take advantage of every opportunity we have in this country. The Mackenzie Delta-Beaufort Sea region is one such area of large new potential, and Canadians simply cannot afford to ignore it. Access to the gas in the Mackenzie-Beaufort is crucial to Canada's energy future. It is
Northern Pipeline
for this reason that I urge an early passage of the bill now before us.
The Alaska highway project will provide Canada with much more than employment and industrial benefits. It will also play a key role in the attainment of our long term energy objectives.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to give my support to this historic piece of legislation. It offers tremendous economic potential for Canada as a whole, including my constituency of Hamilton Mountain and the Hamilton area.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF AGENCY TO SUPERVISE PIPELINE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF AGENCY TO SUPERVISE PIPELINE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
A pipeline would involve 2,000 miles, requiring about 1.3 million tons of steel. The money involved would be about $800 million. It would require about 4,000 man-years to make the steel plate and employ 675 people for four years to turn it into pipe. These are rough figures, but they are very important in my area.
No one can really estimate the demands that would be generated by the increased production of turbines, trucks, housing, etc., associated with a pipeline.
The basic steel and pipe making jobs might be divided between Stelco, Algoma Steel and Ipsco. We are talking about a $700 million order with Arctic gas, and of course we expect to Figure strongly in that, perhaps one million tons for the Hamilton and Welland plants-approximately 3,000 man-years in Hamilton plus several hundred man-years in Welland. Ipsco would probably get the rest in its Regina and Edmonton plants. Dofasco, which would be involved in lighter gauge steel, could not expect that kind of production, but any spinoffs in the auto industry and other industries would benefit. Estimates indicate that at least 100 jobs will be created as a result of the spin-off benefit. All of this is a guessing game, but, after all, it is guessing in the right direction. It is guessing and, 1 hope, working toward a bright new future and toward a technology of which Canada could have command. As we all know, if we ourselves can be involved in the development of that technology, that is where the jobs are. Also the jobs are in the new technology which produces new jobs which the rest of the world can observe.
In addition to the production of pipe for the main lines, there are the 300,000 tons which would be needed for the Dempster. Once Canadian gas was being brought on stream, another 900,000 tons would be needed to expand or loop the TransCanada pipeline. All this depends on the building of the Dempster.
In addition, there is Westinghouse to consider in my area. At least one of their turbines would be used in the pipeline. This is important as a stimulus to Westinghouse overseas sales where difficulties are created by the fact that there are no demonstration projects of its highly efficient equipment in Canada. Even Canadians are overly influenced by foreign technology.
Approximately 90 gas turbines will be needed for the pipeline. Each turbine order Westinghouse receives means about

February 20, 1978
Northern Pipeline
60 man-years for the company in Hamilton. These figures are conservatively estimated but they are very important. When you argue about the pipeline, you should realize that the Deputy Prime Minister and President of Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) is working on behalf of all Canadians. Indeed, it is very appropriate that a man from Cape Breton should be the one who is involved in this, with his negotiating ability, and his ability to talk with a foreign power such as the United States and to discuss with them terms which would achieve an agreement.
Let me say a few words now about job guarantees. We hear much said about job guarantees. Stelco and the rest of the Canadian steel industry want to compete on a purely business like basis. So long as the government enforces anti-dumping regulations and watches out for steel producers from other countries who receive substantial government subsidies, Stelco believes it will get the lion's share of the pipe order. In fact job guarantees can hurt our steel firms since other countries will retaliate with similar guarantees on their projects, thus depriving efficient Hamilton steel firms of the chance to secure international contracts. Stelco and the other Canadian firms want the business, but they want it because they deserve it in terms of service, price, and quality.
Stelco believes in the free enterprise system. It has never said that the pipe must be produced in Canada no matter how high the price. The steel firms are efficient, and the competition for the order, plus the increased production resulting from it, will make them even more so. Surely that is one of the goals of our evolving industrial strategy. I know my comments are narrow, very limited to the Hamilton area. But, after all, that is one of my privileges in representing my constituency, as other hon. members represent theirs. That is not to say that in the larger sense we do not all have a great deal more to say to the rest of Canada and to each other when thinking of the total Canadian situation, but we should not forget that it is important for us in our areas and in our ridings to talk definitely of the benefits that can come from any Canadian project to us, and particularly to our people.
This bill was not developed overnight; it is the culmination of many studies by numerous private sector interests as well as government related bodies. It has been known for years that oil and gas reserves were located in the Arctic. In the 1920's oil wells were drilled at Norman Wells and a U.S. navy petroleum reserve was established in Alaska. However, the remoteness of the area discouraged development in favour of more accessible reserves.
The latest interest in the Arctic occurred following the 1968 discovery by the United States of major oil and gas reserves in the Prudhoe Bay area of Alaska. Interest grew rapidly as the easily tapable reserves ran low. Actually, a year earlier, in 1967, the northwest project study group was formed, and in 1972 it became part of Canadian Arctic Gas Pipeline Limited.
Exploration, production, and transmission companies formed study groups to examine various routes and technolo-

gies involving Prudhoe Bay and the Mackenzie Valley. The federal government as early as 1970 established pipeline guidelines for establishment of a pipeline corridor for oil and gas transmission. It was almost four years ago, in March, 1974, when Chief Justice Berger was appointed to investigate the environmental and social impacts of a Mackenzie Valley pipeline route as proposed by Canadian Arctic Gas.
The National Energy Board held hearings for over a year, from April, 1976, to May, 1977, to consider a northern pipeline to supply U.S. gas to Americans and Canadian gas to Canadians. In July of last year the NEB favoured the Foothills or Yukon Limited proposal along the Alaska Highway with some re-routing and other conditions. It is this proposal which we are considering now, one that is also known as the Alaska Highway project and the Alcan route.
Meanwhile, the Berger Report recommended a ten-year moratorium on a Mackenzie Valley pipeline, and the Lysyk Report concluded that undesirable social and economic consequences could be kept within acceptable limits through several key conditions. Therefore I believe the government has had the pipeline proposal thoroughly studied and has followed closely the various recommendations made. This pipeline route is cheaper, quicker, and will have less environmental impact than the El Paso tanker proposal which the Americans might have undertaken had we not approved the joint line.
The National Energy Board sees Delta gas as the lowest cost new large source of energy over the period 1980 and onward. It considers the environmental and social problems of the Foothills proposal solvable due to the existing transportation corridor, and the National Energy Board points to the key factors of majority Canadian control, no government back stopping, and an accessible construction and supply route.
The figures as to manpower requirements, size, and economic impact are most astounding. It is estimated that, directly and indirectly, the pipeline development will create 100,000 man-years of employment. This includes about 28,000 man-years for construction and 40,000 man-years to manufacturers. The objective-

speechtext:
I did hear one remark, but I do not like to reply when I am reading figures. I am really an arts man and not quite as adept as many others in amassing a great number of figures, but in reply to that interruption about the one million unemployed let me say I always remember the beggar who said "You only dropped a penny but I appreciate it because nobody else dropped anything". I do not think I should knock the jobs that might be created because of the fact people are unemployed. I hope we can create more and more and more, but surely we should not knock the jobs that might be created through the 100,000 man-years.
The project involves construction of 2,765 miles of pipeline in Canada, slightly more than one half of the total of 5,487 miles. Cost of construction in Canada is estimated at $4.2
February 20, 1978

billion, excluding the Dempster lateral, or almost one half of the $10 billion estimated total cost of the pipeline.
The government is not rushing into this enormous project, yet is placing all urgency on keeping a tentative schedule of construction commencement in 1980-81 in northern B.C. and the Yukon, together with a start on pipeline laying in the Yukon by January, 1981. The beginning of operations is expected by January, 1983.
I am saying, coming from my area and thinking of the jobs the hon. member opposite mentioned, it is not too soon to start immediately building stockpiles. I say that knowing my voice will be listened to and considered by as honourable a man as the Deputy Prime Minister, who is concerned about Canadians. Let us start the stockpiles as soon as possible, let us start the storehouses of pipes because we need them all across the country so that we will have the pipe when we commence the pipeline.
It is significant to note that a northern pipeline agency is to be created to maximize economic benefits and minimize social and environmental impacts. Legislative powers now exercised by several other governmental departments and agencies will be transferred to the northern pipeline agency in order to create a single regulatory authority over this project. Designs, specifications, and routing will be subject to approval by this federal agency.
I will not repeat in detail the administrative plans which include a designated officer and a deputy head in Ottawa, together with an administrator in Calgary responsible for day-to-day operations. Foothills (Yukon) is required to cover the cost of this agency and the National Energy Board planning and overseeing until one year after project completion. The minister responsible for the project will be undertaking consultations with the United States, the provinces and the territories in Canada concerned, in order to co-ordinate all aspects of this project. An immediate appeal procedure will be provided through the Federal Court of Appeal.
Companies involved in the project will be required to provide extensive information on such matters as cost, financing, and shipper producer contracts. In the words of the Deputy Prime Minister, "the effort will be to maximize Canadian input and also look after the critical interest of Canadian gas consumers in seeing that the pipeline is built as efficiently and cheaply as possible".
Indeed, consumers in Canada will have a relatively greater stake in the pipeline than their American counterparts. By the mid-1980's Arctic gas will supply about 10 per cent of our domestic needs while Alaska gas will supply only about 5 per cent of the United States needs.
There is ample provision in the legislation to protect the interests of the Yukon. The territory will receive up to $200 million against future tax liability, and $35 million in property taxes before completion of the project. In addition, Foothills will be required to spend up to $5 million for lateral lines to supply gas to areas along the route. Preference will be given to
Northern Pipeline
Yukon residents in training and hiring for construction and operation of the pipeline.
Access to Mackenzie Delta reserves provided for in this legislation is an important part of our national strategy. Provisions in the bill call for the lateral to be ready to go when the need arises to draw on this frontier gas. The pipeline should provide a strong stimulus to further exploration in this area.
I must note that Canada and the United States, through this pipeline agreement, already overwhelmingly approved by the U.S. Congress, have joined in one of the largest private projects ever undertaken to satisfy the pressing energy needs of consumers of both countries. This, we all hope, will be the basis of further co-operation between the United States and Canada.
If there were no agreement with the United States on this pipeline it is unlikely there would be any opportunity in the future for us to gain access to Delta gas reserves. As my colleague, the President of Privy Council, said, the pipeline project will provide a "substantial stimulus to Canadian production and employment and assist in the achievement of Canada's national goal of energy self-reliance."
This will give Canadian personnel and suppliers full opportunity to compete in goods and services for the construction of the project. It should provide a needed boost to consumer and business confidence in both Canada and the United States. Our balance of payments position will get support through capital inflows to this country and tariffs on American gas transported through the Canadian system.
Canadian companies sought no monopoly, as would have been inherent in a guaranteed percentage of Canadian content. As the Deputy Prime Minister said, we have in this country highly developed companies in these fields that have requested no more than a fair and competitive opportunity to participate in the supply of goods and services for the pipeline.
I should like to echo the comments of the hon. member for Welland (Mr. Railton) when he indicated that we should build this pipeline cheaply, efficiently, and make certain there are no unnecessary delays. In today's economy, delays cost dearly, considering what inflation can do to the construction dollar. The hon. member for Welland also indicated that Canadian companies are not worried about the thickness of the pipe, or about its diameter and whether it is high or low pressure. We should get on with this debate, without undue attention being paid to needless haranguing.
We have shown that our friends to the south are indeed our friends. We have shown that we have the kind of person who can deal in a foreign affairs manner not only with the President of the United States but with many of his representatives. It is a proud moment for me, representing the riding of Hamilton Mountain, to stand with the Deputy Prime Minister, a man from Cape Breton, who has stood so strongly for Canadians and who is now able to bring forward a proposal in a bill which will produce many, many jobs for Canadians in the future.

February 20, 1978
Northern Pipeline

He made a lot of observations which indicated that he has been reading the policies put forward by my party, as well as correcting his previous position. I see the minister for unemployment is chuckling. Perhaps he should read the last few publications of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, in particular the energy policy of 1973 and the energy strategy which followed. If he did so, he would notice a remarkable change in view from what the government published as a policy and what was articulated today. We welcome that change in view, but four years have been lost. Government members should have read our speeches earlier.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources indicated that the pipeline would provide easier access to Delta gas. In view of uncertain world supplies, uncertain domestic supplies in southern Canada, uncertain political situations and so on, he indicated that it would be necessary to use that gas. I could not agree more. It is vitally important, but more important is the land use regulations, the royalty structures, the permit structures, and the licensing structures which will pertain to noth-ern Canadian lands under federal jurisdiction. Canada can have the most beautiful pipeline in the world, but it cannot deliver anything unless someone explores for stocks of oil and gas to fill the pipeline. That will not happen unless the government does something soon with respect to royalty structures in the Northwest Territories and the High Arctic.
The royalty regulations which were brought in by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) were kept in place until April, 1970. At that time the government withdrew them and indicated that it would be making changes. Approximately Vh years later the government introduced a new set of regulations which are totally hopeless in terms of encouraging exploration. These were introduced last August through an order in council. If anyone makes a cursory

examination of what is happening in the north he will find that exploration is tailing off substantially. The people of that region realize a pipeline company is coming, but exploration is not being increased by them because, under the present rules, it is not worth attempting to find oil and gas in the north.
The minister has indicated quite accurately that Canada needs oil and gas to satisfy its needs and to protect us from the vagaries and uncertainties of a world which is running short and is politically uncertain in some areas. When he makes that case he should realize that for anyone to have confidence in the government it is necessary to put rules and regulations in place which will encourage industry representatives to find oil and gas in the north.
I see the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources is re-entering the Chamber. He seemed to state a new policy of the government, but it was previously articulated on this side of the House, namely, that the nation should pursue an energy policy of displacing the consumption of crude oil with natural gas.

speechtext:
I have just found out that the hon. minister has been reading the speeches of Conservative members. I am pleased to see a change of mind on the part of the minister. The minister had great confidence in the exploration activities taking place in southern Canada, and in particular in Alberta. He indicated that those activities were producing fair volumes of natural gas. He expressed the thought that we could not rely on that effort to produce all our gas requirements, and that we would need more from the High Arctic and offshore.
In his discussion of the so-called gas bubble in Alberta and the exploration effort there, the minister failed to acknowledge that many of the explorers are small Canadian companies, the so-called independents. These companies are without large cash flows from existing production. They raise their money to a large extent through new investment and, as such, do not have the capability of discovering reserves of gas and leaving them for five, ten or 20 years, until such time as the market opens up so that they can sell them. In other words, they need cash flow from their discoveries in order to finance further exploration.
Waiting until 1983 or 1985 or beyond-until 1990-when Delta gas may be brought down to pursue this policy of replacement of natural gas and to work toward increasing the consumption of natural gas as opposed to crude oil, has the effect of denying these independents cash flow at this point in time when they are able to go out, and want to go out, to continue to explore and discover more gas. What I am leading up to is that if the minister felt, and was genuine in his feeling, that it is in our interest as a nation to pursue replacement of crude oil with natural gas, in other words, to increase the total proportion of national consumption of gas-we should be negotiating a swap arrangement with the United States right now or accelerating existing exports in order to provide these
February 20, 1978

small independents with cash flows so that they can maintain their current, aggressive exploration efforts.
I am absolutely convinced that these small independents need more cash flow. Let us remember that with a swap arrangement or an acceleration of existing exports we do not at all diminish our long term security position. We simply provide cash flow at this point to those who are demonstrably using it to find more gas, so in fact we increase our security by finding more natural gas. If it is government policy that Canadians will use more natural gas, this seems a logical and sensible extension, and I hope the minister will pursue that policy.
We hope Bill C-25 will eventually lead to the construction of this pipeline, but as we look back at the process involved, expressions like "horrendously expensive", "political sham", "world's largest poker game" and "hodge-podge" come to mind. When we look back at the whole process the overwhelming impression which is left is one of incredible size and magnitude. It has been an incredibly inefficient way to reach a decision. The costs have been staggering. Canadian Arctic Gas is estimated to have spent $130 million on its unsuccessful attempt to secure the right to bring Prudhoe gas to the United States border. It is estimated that the Foothills group spent about $40 million. If we add up all the money spent by the National Energy Board, the Berger Commission, the Lysyk Commission, and internal government operations, it is not unreasonable to come up with a total of about $250 million in basically a non-productive exercise. Granted, some money was spent on accumulating engineering knowledge which will be used in the pipeline project, but only a small portion. The remainder was spent just on reaching this decision. If we had the same kind of decision-making process then as we do now, I wonder if we would ever have had the CPR.
There have been some suggestions, although they are abating these days, that the National Energy Board made a political decision as opposed to a technical or correct one. Frankly, I have read the documentation quite thoroughly and I find little evidence of that. I do not think such a position can be substantiated, but there is an extremely unfortunate perception of the integrity of the National Energy Board when we consider the way the decision was made. 1 hope that never again will we have in this country two or three separate boards or inquiries looking into the same question.
The government should be eternally thankful that the NEB did not make a recommendation contrary to the recommendation of Mr. Justice Berger because, if there had been two or more government commissions or boards making opposite decisions, the political chaos would have made life just a little uncomfortable. I wonder what discussions have taken place in the cabinet in this regard, and I wonder what decision-making process was involved.
We have had various ministers stating various things. One stated that no pipeline can be built until land claims are settled. Another stated that land claims settlements are quite a separate question and that one does not necessarily have to precede the other. In his speech on the resolution introduced
Northern Pipeline
by the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) last August, my leader referred to what I think is an "Alice in Wonderland" attitude with regard to the decision-making process. My leader said the following:
Mr. Justice Berger, having studied the Mackenzie Valley route, prefers the Alcan route, which he has not studied. The NEB, having studied Berger, recommends access to the Dempster route, which it has not studied. The Lysyk group, the third inquiry in a venture conceived, originally, to achieve Canadian access to the Canadian reserves, recommends a route which gives American access to American reserves, with the possibility of connection to Canadian reserves, assuming the viability of the Dempster connection, which nobody has studied.
The way which has been used to arrive at a decision is incredibly complex and bizarre. The only thing more bizarre is the way in which the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has assigned responsibility. One might describe the northern pipeline as a northern development project, yet the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Faulkner) has not had any responsibility, nor did the previous minister, the current Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Allmand).
If it is not a northern project, it seems logical that it could be an energy project. Indeed the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources did try to negotiate a pipeline treaty with the United States about two years ago. However, when the resolution of the House of Commons was passed and when the decision of the NEB came down and it was time for the government to sit down with our friends and neighbours, the Americans, to negotiate a pipeline treaty, it was not the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources who participated. It was not the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson), even though international relations would normally come under his authority. It was not the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner), even though trade and commerce are related to this.

speechtext:
I see the Deputy Prime Minister nodding in agreement but I do not think that little sham will turn the attention of the people away from the performance of this government over the last ten years. We are not worried about the outcome of the election, whatever it may be. I am confident we will be given the responsibility of clearing up this mess within the next few months.
This is an important project for Canada and we want to co-operate. In August we agreed that the pipeline should go

through, and we have not changed our view. Several members on this side have given details of things we would like to see modified in the bill. We hope there will be more flexibility and willingness to co-operate when it reaches committee than have yet been demonstrated by the government. We want to pass the bill with dispatch and efficiency and this is possible if there is a willingness to co-operate on the other side. If that is not the case, however, it may take some time for the bill to go through. That would be unfortunate for the country, but it would not be the fault of this side.
This project is important for the country psychologically, Mr. Speaker. It is a $10 billion project, but we must remember that the Canadian portion only amounts to $3.8 billion. It is not as complex, for example, as the Syncrude tar sands plant in terms of the technology, the construction and environmental impact. The hon. member for Hamilton-Mountain referred to exciting new technology but, Mr. Speaker, it is the oldest technology in the world. As a matter of fact, building pipelines is a simple engineering task, and Canada is probably one of the world's best at it. We can do it quickly, effectively, and more efficiently than any other country. We are also in the forefront of the communications industry, so to describe this as some big research and development project just is not correct. It is something that Canada has been doing well for a number of years and we have no need to be frightened of it.
A very small portion of the project will go into territory that has not had pipeline before, and that is the part in the Yukon. Northern British Columbia has all kinds of pipeline already so they know how to lay and maintain pipe. It is not a frontier in any sense of the word. Alberta has thousands of miles of pipe. Indeed, I think the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave) probably has more pipe running under his ranch than will be running in territory that has not been pipelined before. We have no need to be concerned about the magnitude of the project.
I wonder why the National Energy Board, or the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, or the President of Privy Council has not referred to the Energy Resources Conservation Board in Alberta or its equivalent in British Columbia for guidance on the operation and management of the project. Both provinces have thousands of miles of pipe. This would seem to be a good area for federal-provincial co-operation, and since these provinces already have the expertise, their help could mean a substantial saving in expenses.
A stimulus of $4 billion to the Canadian economy is of great importance but I want to point out, particularly to members of the New Democratic Party, that the money will not be spent primarily in British Columbia, Alberta, or even the Yukon. Most of it will be spent in the rest of the country.
Some years ago an economist at McGill University undertook a study of what happens to a dollar spent for oil exploration in Alberta. Some 65 cents of that dollar ended up in central Canada in the hands of suppliers, bankers, and transportation companies. That is from oil exploration only. For pipelining, the spread of money will be much larger. Out of that $4 billion a very large percentage will end up in other
February 20, 1978

regions of the country apart from where the pipeline itself is located. With co-operation for the government, the benefits of the pipeline could easily be expanded into Quebec and Atlantic Canada where there is a real need for jobs today. The government could help in locating suppliers, removing transportation bottlenecks and in acquainting producers and manufacturers and service operations with the opportunities; the government could bring together the contractors and the suppliers from Atlantic Canada and Quebec, and this could ease the serious unemployment problems they are experiencing.
The government could do a lot toward spreading the benefits of this project right across the country. That is what I would call positive government action. That is the sort of effort it should be directing itself toward now. It does not need legislation, or new hiring of hundreds of civil servants. It does not need to create new authorities or regulations. All that is required is for the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Les-sard) to get to work and do their jobs. They can spread the wealth across the country.
Another aspect of this project I will just touch on because it will be discussed in greater detail by my friend, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton). I am sure the Deputy Prime Minister and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources have heard of the proposal from this party to provide an opportunity to Canadians to participate in the equity position of this pipeline. It will be a good investment. There has never been any pipeline which has lost money. However, that is not to say pipelines are free from risks, they are not.
Who will have the chance to invest in this venture? Clearly the Foothills and AGTL group have put a lot of money into this project and they deserve an opportunity to participate. If other people are to be given an opportunity to participate in the profits and equity position, to whom should it be given? Our proposal, as the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain will point out, is that all Canadians should be given that opportunity as was the case in 1957 when the government of Alberta gave its citizens the opportunity to participate in the Alberta Gas Trunk Line shares when that company was formed.
In fact if members opposite would read my speech on February 2, an allotted day, they will see that this party is encouraging that kind of approach to be used in many activities. Instead of creating Crown corporations or granting special privileges to special groups, use the Alberta Gas Trunk Line model and let individual Canadians participate in the equity position.
The hon. member for Yukon in leading off our party's debate on this issue indicated the importance of parliamentary monitoring of the activities of the pipeline authority. One aspect of this bill troubles me. That is the discretionary authority given to government. It is a typical theme which is included in a lot of legislation put forward by this government.
Northern Pipeline
We find it offensive in general for governments to ask parliament to give them discretionary authority to do whatever they want. It is a principle which the government applies far too frequently. It may be too late to do anything in this regard now, but one of the checks we can impose is that of parliamentary monitoring of what is happening. It is an after the fact method, that through knowledge the activities of government will be exposed to the light of day through a parliamentary committee. We feel that it will provide a control on potential abuses or misuses of the power we will be granting by the passage of this bill. We strongly recommend that when this bill goes to committee the government give favourable consideration to our amendments in this regard.
We do not intend to delay this bill, Mr. Speaker. We think the project is important and we think it will have tremendous advantage to Canada. It is important to Canada's long term energy situation. The process the government used in coming to this point was abysmal, to say the least. It was extremely costly and chaotic. It took it a long time to arrive at this juncture. We do not quite understand how the Prime Minister could have an energy minister and yet not allow that minister to have anything to do with the largest energy project that this country has ever undertaken. We cannot understand why an energy minister would take that slap in the face and not resign.
Finally, I take off my MP's hat and put on my chemical engineer's ring and talk about a 56-inch pipeline. I cannot see how the National Energy Board could have arrived at any other decision. Once they had decided on capacities, the size was dictated. To have gone to a higher pressure pipeline would have represented a step out in terms of technology that had too many risks associated with it. The problem, in my opinion as an engineer, is less pipe than it is everything else-valves, fittings, compressors. I am sure we can build a pipe, weld it and install it, a pipe which will withstand those kinds of pressures. We do not know how much extra precautions would be necessary and therefore costs might escalate. There are always unforeseen costs in making that kind of technological advance.
Frankly, as an engineer, what would have scared me most of all in choosing these very high pressure pipes was the questions of valves, compressors, etc. This is especially so in the northern sectors where there are extreme climate changes. It is difficult to have equipment that will operate properly even under moderate situations. When you experience great temperature changes and a technological step like that is made to very high pressures, the risks are inordinate.
The 56-inch size pipe, of course, is based on a decision to provide now for the capacity to bring down Delta gas through the Dempster line. Having made that decision there is no reason for any delay in proceeding with the study of the Dempster Highway connection to the Mackenzie Delta. If you are installing 56-inch pipe it is because you expect the Dempster lateral to be built. They follow one after another. It would be stupid to instal 56-inch pipe if there was a significant possibility that the Dempster lateral would not be built. Money would be wasted. By adopting a 56-inch pipe the government is
