speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this debate. I wish to make a few comments on Bill C-25 for the building of the Alcan pipeline. It will be the largest and costliest in the history of this country and will have far reaching implications, particularly for those in the north, far reaching, socially, politically, economically, and environmentally.
My colleagues in the New Democratic Party have raised a number of very serious issues in this debate. I join with them in stating that, as the pipeline legislation now stands, this project will be one of the biggest sellouts in our history. If that happens to be the case, there are not many of us here today who will be proud to have been a part of allowing that to happen.
A great deal has been said during the debate on the economic aspects of building the pipeline. I strongly support the criticisms of the legislation that have been made by my colleagues. I am not happy that the government has introduced this bill at this time as it offers no guarantee that this project will generate jobs for Canadian workers. I say this particularly in view of the fact that there are now over one million people in this country who are unemployed.
There is only one guarantee in the legislation. That is that within a few years time a pipeline will run through Canada moving American gas to American markets. As the bill now stands, that is the only guarantee.
Leaving aside the economic issues for a moment, I wish to address a few remarks to the human aspects of this legislation. This area of concern has received very little attention. The government seems to have overlooked this important fact. I refer to those who live along the proposed route in the Yukon, northern British Columbia and northern Alberta. They are the ones who will bear the brunt of this project both during and after construction.
I do not know how to get this fact across to the government. Following their planned show in Alberta in March of this year, perhaps it would help if the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his travelling cabinet visited Whitehorse and other parts of the Yukon. In any event, the lives of those in that part of the country will be very deeply affected by the building of this pipeline.
The impact on the local economy will be disruptive and lasting. How will the people of the Yukon minimize the adverse effects of the project on the people themselves and the economy as it is now?
There is no way the Alcan pipeline can be justified in terms of benefit to the local economy. It cannot be justified in terms

of benefits it will bring to people of the Yukon. It appears the Yukon communities will not even benefit from cheap fuel supplies as a result of the pipeline. There will be the same situation as occurred in Alaska. That pipeline brought Alaskan gas past the doorsteps of people who paid very high rates for fuel to heat their homes. It was exported to the lower 48 and they had to buy it back. That is exactly what will happen to the Yukon.
The Foothills construction schedule calls for roughly 2,000 or more workers to be employed on pipeline construction during the peak period, and the majority of these workers will come from outside the Yukon. Although the Yukon Territorial government is making some preparations to see that Y ukoners will be hired for work on the project, the job situation remains in a shaky position. We have no real guarantees that Yukoners will be given preference in hiring. The skilled construction workers necessary for pipeline work do not exist in the Yukon and Northwest Territories.
All we have is a statement by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) that he expects arrangements will be made with the pipeline companies to have interested Yukon residents sent out for training and experience on pipeline jobs. This is definitely not the kind of guarantee on which people in the Yukon and Northwest Territories, especially in the western Arctic along the Mackenzie Valley, can rely.
Furthermore, it seems very unrealistic that the companies are going to lay off skilled pipeline workers who have been involved in the project in the southern section in British Columbia and Alberta when they reach the Yukon border because of some definition which states that these workers are not sourdoughs.
There are no guarantees that Yukon workers will have first crack at pipeline jobs. The government has not said how it plans to enforce any regulations that will guarantee jobs to people in the Yukon and Northwest Territories. Nothing in the legislation is strong enough. If those in government have given this serious thought since debate on this bill started, perhaps we will hear about that today or within the next few days.
Yukon communities will have to accommodate the needs of in-migrants at considerable financial and social cost. Most of the workers will leave the Yukon when the project is finished. We have seen that happen time and again. It happened with the building of DEW line sites, the town of Inuvik, and the building of a few gravel highways. What was left behind was usually not good.
During construction of the Alyeska pipeline in Alaska, the influx of people led to the disruption of local economies, an increased demand for government and commercial services, and a rate of inflation that was double the United States rate of inflation at the time the pipeline was built. There is no sensible reason to suggest that the Yukon experience will be any different.
Surely we have something to learn from the Alaskan experience. During the period of pipeline construction several important changes occurred in the city of Fairbanks, for example.
February 20, 1978

This affected drastically the lives of the local people. Unemployment rose, prices went up, nearly one half the work force suffered a loss of real income, taxes increased, and inflation went crazy.
Migration into a community causes serious shortages. There is an increased demand for services, utilities, and commodities, not excluding housing. This is what the people of Whitehorse, one of the largest communities along the route of the proposed pipeline, have to look forward to now. There is no way in which one can justify the building of the pipeline in terms of benefits it will bring to people of the north.
The Lysyk inquiry clearly stated:
The Foothills project relative to the Yukon economy is at least comparable to the size of the Alyeska pipeline in relation to the Alaskan economy.
Is this what the government has in mind for the people of the Yukon-higher prices, unemployment, and a drop in real income? For example, public service accounts for between 25 and 30 per cent of the Yukon work force. Public servants have endured the inflation of recent years. They have been obliged to pay steadily increasing rents because no rent controls were enacted in the Yukon, even after the formation of the AntiInflation Board. Now public servants may be left out in the cold, their wages frozen despite the rapid inflation we can expect in the local economy during the construction period.
Evidence before the Lysyk inquiry suggested that a significant increase in the cost of living in the Yukon could be expected while wage increases would not be uniform. This was the experience in the Fairbanks area of Alaska. Incidentally, I understand that banks, police forces, and even schools were affected by the project. People left their jobs to take on temporary work at higher pay. Police forces lost some of their men who preferred to take on jobs as security officers along the route. This is not the kind of thing which brings long lasting benefit to an area.
There is only one Canadian city where the cost of living is higher than in Whitehorse and that is Yellowknife in the Northwest Territories. However, it seems the people of Yellowknife can expect to lose that dubious distinction because the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) and his collegues seem determined to ensure that Whitehorse experiences the highest cost of living in Canada; he and his party want this legislation even more than do members on the government side of the House.
So far I have not mentioned the social problems. We shall be facing many of these in the building of this pipeline. It is inevitable that social problems will accompany high unemployment, a loss of real income, increased abuse of alcohol, increased drug abuse, prostitution, family breakdown, mental strain and, most probably, increased criminal activity resulting from in-migration into the Yukon.
Health, social and educational services will be strained to the breaking point and beyond. Most of these services are already strained to the limits of their capacity. Government services will expand, and the people of the Yukon will end up
Adjournment Motion
paying for them. During the construction of the Alaska Highway the Yukon witnessed the effect of the migration of some 30,000 people. One presentation to the Lysyk inquiry estimated that as many as 30,000 people could be drawn into the Yukon during the peak period of pipeline construction. Whitehorse still bears traces of the planning problems which were encountered as a result of the building of the Alaska Highway some 30 years ago.
Today, Whitehorse is a city of some 12,000 people. I remember when they extended the boundaries. They boasted about being one of the largest cities, in area, in Canada. Whitehorse has an area of about 162 square miles, and the operation and maintenance of services in such an area require considerable expenditure. So services will be strained to their limit, or beyond, during the peak period of the building of the pipeline.
I have mentioned the Lysyk inquiry several times. I should now like to ask this question: what has happened to the recommendations of that inquiry? In the short space of just three months the commission was able to respond quite effectively to the concern of those living in the Yukon by putting forward a number of specific recommendations. First, what happened to the undertaking to hold a second stage inquiry? I would remind the government that the native people and the environmental groups took part in that inquiry on condition that there would be a further investigation, a second stage inquiry. The government promised that such an inquiry would be forthcoming, bearing in mind that Lysyk had only three months in which to do his work.
May I call it five o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of establishing a western Canada development centre to assemble and monitor, on a continuing basis, data concerning energy, construction, transportation, investment, housing, education and population as the basis for federal and provincial government policies to ensure integrated economic and social development in western Canada; such centre to be funded by a partnership of the federal, western provincial and northern governments and business, labour and academic bodies, who would prepare an annual report and public conference on growth in western Canada.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the focus of my address this afternoon in this private members' hour is on improving the quality of life in western Canada, not just the quantity. The new west contains within its vast areas perhaps the highest potential for personal fulfilment the world has ever known, provided we find a way to integrate economic and social planning to make a more human society.
When I use the phrase "new west", I mean the four western provinces, the Yukon, the Northwest Territories, a region that covers 70 per cent of the total land area of Canada and has a population of six million, or 27 per cent of the population of Canada as a whole. Here is found 80 per cent of Canadian farmland, more than half the merchantable timber, and almost all the proven economic reserves and potential resources of oil and gas.	-
By now everyone has heard that the new west has taken off on an economic boom so strong that the financial centre of gravity in Canada is moving westward. The list of construction projects is dazzling. They involve the $10 billion Alcan gas pipeline, which the House is now debating, the largest private construction project in history; the $2.15 billion Syncrude plant at Fort McMurray, now almost ready to start oil sands
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Turner).]
production; the $2.5 billion steam injection oil sands plant to be built at Cold Lake; huge coal and uranium mining projects, and petrochemical plants.
These energy projects are truly spectacular, but the new west is more than a storehouse of mineral resources. It has an enormous food production capacity, an unlimited supply of fresh water, and growing entrepreneurial and management skills. The benefits are already felt throughout British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba where the gross provincial product for the four provinces in 1976 was $8,850 per capita, which exceeded the Ontario and Quebec per capita of $8,280.
It is clear that the economic balance of power in Canada has shifted. We have the resources, the technology, the talent, and the money to keep expanding. The Alberta Heritage Fund has accumulated nearly $3 billion and will soon be growing at the rate of $1 billion a year. The new west is an attractive investment, and thus we are emerging as the principal economic force in Canada. In fact the strength of Canada as a whole now depends on the west. Last fall's Financial Post conference on western Canadian development, "Think West", was well named.
Western development is all the more remarkable considering that national economic policies have always been directed to the benefit of central Canada. The development of federally assisted petrochemical plants in the industrial heartland of Ontario, rather than policies directed toward upgrading at the source, is but one example. Inequitable freight rates have been a longstanding sore in western Canada.
Our resources in energy have enabled the west to emerge, but the new wealth will prove fleeting if industrial diversification does not follow. The west needs more industrial and processing diversity to upgrade and add value to its rich agricultural and resource base, to provide permanent jobs and business stability, to avoid vulnerability to big-project boom-or-bust cycles and the growing instability of farm and other primary product prices. This is why Alberta's premier, Peter Lougheed, is now calling for a new national economic policy involving "co-operative federalism in the fullest sense of mutually agreed upon economic policy and direction".
The idea of co-operation is well understood in western Canada. Indeed the western provinces have found sufficient common ground on which to base a lasting environment for strong co-operation and collaboration. The most prominent rallying point among the western provinces which sparks this co-operative spirit is our desire to pursue the economic destiny which we feel is ours. By having the opportunity to develop to our fullest potential, the western provinces feel this is the manner in which we can make the maximum contribution to Confederation.
Reviewing the history of western provincial co-operation, Dr. Gerry T. Gartner has written in Canadian Public Administration that it is becoming increasingly more difficult for a single province to muster the resources necessary to research, plan, and develop policies and programs. "To some
February 20, 1978

extent, western provincial co-operation is a creature of necessity".
As far back as the first meeting of the prairie economic council in 1965, the western governments have seen the benefits of co-ordinating economic development policies on a regional basis. The one prairie province conference in Lethbridge in 1970 focused on wide constitutional, political, social, economic, and regional development issues. When the Western Economic Opportunities Conference was held in 1973 the west was ready to present Ottawa with a single regional position on agricultural, energy, and transportation policies that transcended their diverse political ideologies.
The Western Economic Opportunities Conference was not, of course, a flaming political, or economic, success. But it showed westerners themselves, as well as Ottawa, the shared common interests in the west. All four provinces want greater interprovincial trade and a larger role in Canada's export of manufactured goods. They want an efficient, economic, and stable grain handling and shipping system. They want a shared power of determination in federal-provincial cost-sharing programs. Undoubtedly the future of Canadian federalism will depend, in large part, on the resolution of these problems which threaten national unity.
Because of gains through co-operative economic analysis, it is distressing to note that similar progress has not been made on issues that have a social theme. Dr. Gartner and other analysts have concluded that the least effective co-operation is found in the social area: social policy, cultural policy, educational policy and justice. Topics such as social service costs, native problems, billingualism, school curriculum content, and corrections and law reform have been discussed by the western premiers, but little in the way of co-operation has resulted. This is unfortunate because the spectacular economic growth of western Canada is obscuring deep social problems. The evidence is mounting to convince anyone who still needs convincing that economic growth alone does not make a healthy or beneficial society.
Consider just the situation in Alberta which is the cutting edge of western growth. In 1976 Alberta led the nation in the rate of both drugs and sexual offences and in violent crimes. Drug offences jumped 55.8 per cent over the preceding year. The rate of sexual offences, 60.57 per 100,000 population, was well above the national rate of 46.07.
Social problems are by no means confined to the criminal element. Though Alberta is one of the most blessed spots in the whole world, the divorce, alcoholism, abortion, and suicide rates are the highest in the country. There is discrimination against native peoples. Welfare rolls have soared. Major transportation bottlenecks have occurred in Edmonton and Calgary. Real estate prices and rentals have risen at unconscionable rates. Farmers are alarmed at the rate at which prime farmland is being gobbled up by housing and industrial developments. There is a desperate shortage of accommodation for senior citizens. Four thousand people a month are migrating to Alberta in search of jobs; and because the western boom is principally technological, not labor-intensive, many unskilled
Western Canada Development Centre
and semi-skilled remain unemployed, thus swelling the demand for social services.
In the midst of boom, there is not enough money for social services. What a paradox! Is it any wonder that family breakdown has become the most serious social problem of our time despite new-found wealth? As the Edmonton Journal drily observed:
We have not been very successful in coping with the negative aspects of economic growth.
It is imperative that we upgrade the quality of life in western Canada by more attention to the social factors affected by economic boom. The problem is not wealth; the problem is people: people being increasingly excluded from what should be the real benefits of wealth while a few are increasingly favored. It is undeniable that people in all walks of life feel excluded from work, from status, from identity, from meaningful living.
When I talk about "quality of life" I am not talking about some vague comfort. I mean those areas that are regarded internationally as social indicators of the quality of life: health, individual development through learning, employment and quality of working life, leisure, command over goods and services, physical environment, personal safety and the administration of justice, and social opportunity and equality.
In the development of Canada so far, the accent necessarily has been on building and growth. Our success has been measured in the production of goods and services. But the conditions of modern society have changed dramatically in the past few years as a result of the technological and cultural explosions. Technology has brought many benefits-communications and transportation are just two examples-but it has also been a chief source of anxiety and spreading frustration that characterize modern life. The acquisition of more goods has not by itself made us a happier people.
Affluence makes sense only if it leads to increased social justice and personal fulfilment. In this way economic growth may become a means to the end of an enhanced quality of life. We are not without human concern in our institutions including this one, but we frequently express it in the wrong way. We add on humanizing factors to public policy rather than starting from the base of the human being, his rights and dignity. Our social security policies in pensions and unemployment insurance allocations are a prime example of this "adding on" humanization. In other words, we create a system which generates casualties and then add on another huge system to compensate the casualties.
These disorders stem from a distortion of values. The value of the human being is measured by his ability to buy, and hence consume. Those who are materially poor have failed. Measuring the worth of persons by their income level and buying power encourages social discrimination that compounds that harm. A subtle discrimination segregates rich and poor in housing developments, schools, law enforcement and health care. It is easy to enunciate a clear principle of justice:

February 20, 1978
Western Canada Development Centre
every member of the Canadian society has a right to a share of the national wealth sufficient to enable him to participate fully in society. But it is very difficult to put this principle into practice while there is so much public confusion and resentment of the present social security system.
A more human society in Western Canada cannot be brought about solely by the relentless march of technology any more than by unfettered individualism. It can only be brought about by an orderly co-operative approach in which the individual and special interest give way to public concern for the common good. As Harleigh B. Trecker points out in "Goals for Social Welfare", 1973-1993,
The individual must be seen and understood in society in a much more complete way than in the past. The intervening act of helping must focus not only on the individual but on the interaction of the individual in his groups and in society. Many of the pressures on the individual are societal in origin and no amount of working on or with the individual alone can relieve these pressures. Society must be changed.
We have to begin somewhere. The new west, because it is a dynamic that will affect all of Canada, is the place to start. I am calling for the development of an indepandent organization that will not only analyze the economic factors of growth in the four western provinces and the north but will promote sound social policies. It must speak courageously of values and desirable social objectives, but remember that resources are not unlimited. It must remain non-partisan but skilled in the work of governments which have the final responsibility for public economic and social policy. The organization must have enough financial support to operate with a high degree of professional competence.
In short, the time has come to co-ordinate systematically all the data concerning energy, construction, agriculture, transportation, investment, housing, education and population so that a clear picture emerges of what is happening to society in western Canada. Then, as my motion proposes, this complete picture would serve as the basis for federal and provincial government policies to ensure integrated economic and social development in the west.
Here I wish to pay tribute to the Canada West Foundation, a small, independent group of business leaders formed four years ago in Calgary to conduct research programs into western problems and to stimulate greater public awareness of the future of the west. Headed by Arthur J. E. Child, President of Burns Foods Ltd., the Foundation concentrates on an orderly development of the resources of the west. It has so far completed eleven research projects and its study of the energy and mineral resources of Canada is the definitive work on the subject. In process now are studies on agriculture, water resources and coal. Valuable though it is, Canada West Foundation, as Mr. Child himself has described it, is "an elitist organization" because it is small and highly specialized. Nonetheless, it is not a closed organization and its executive director, L. A. Thorssen, recognizes that a wider approach is necessary for material and human development and says: a co-ordinated and well-planned, total Canadian strategy could provide all Canadians with an enhanced quality of life.

The aims of the organization I envisage are contained in the name I am proposing: a Western Canada Development Centre. For me the word development signifies not only things but persons. Development means not only acquisition but victory over social scourges; the growth of knowledge, an expression of culture. Development is a whole. It is an integral, value-loaded, cultural process. It encompasses the natural environment, social relations, education, production, consumption and wellbeing. The development I seek for western Canada is an integral humanism. This requires the involvement of business, churches, universities, ethnic groups, credit unions, social agencies and others.
I should like to refer to one example of a human problem looming in the west. An economic boom has traditionally meant jobs. The trek of the unemployed to the west is well under way, but the chief characteristic of the new boom is that it is capital intensive and not labour intensive.

Mr. Speaker, I thank hon. members for their co-operation. The major projects require more than $1 million of investment for each job created. Because of the boom, people are trekking west for jobs only to find that it is a capital intensive boom and not the kind which creates many permanent jobs. Construction jobs to start up resource extraction are short lived. No wonder the Alberta labour movement wants permanent secure jobs which will allow the work force to live the kind of meaningful, dignified, and orderly community life which we all have the full right to expect. I believe the answer to this problem is found in the housing construction industry, which is the greatest source of long term jobs.
Family formation and earning power are strong factors in the west. What is needed to stimulate the housing industry is better mortgage financing and more government action to make land available for housing. There is a joint responsibility of private enterprise and government to do an in depth assessment of the kind of industrial growth which will support future breadwinners and be good for family life. That is one example to indicate the integration between economic and social development. On one hand, the economic factors which have led to this boom are studied and, on the other hand, what the boom does to family life is studied, as well as what should be done to help family life achieve the true benefits of the boom.
In this new economic era the west will be challenged as never before to create secure jobs and to maintain stable communities. Public participation in the work of the Western Canada Development Centre is therefore essential. This can best be promoted through the publication of an annual report on the west by the development centre, which would provide the basis for an annual public conference to enable a flow of ideas and reactions concerning western growth to reach gov-
February 20, 1978

eminent leaders. Parenthetically, should the west really have to depend on the eastern based Financial Post to hold a conference in the west to tell them about themselves?
It is possible to tap the knowledge and wisdom of a wide range of individuals and organizations in western Canada whose common goal would be to promote the development of the new west as a centre of excellence. Canada West Foundation could indeed be a core group. The information already acquired on the people, land and heritage of the west by the Canadian Plains Research Centre at the University of Regina would surely be a valuable academic basis.
With a credible community base, a flow of funding should be available from the federal, western provincial and northern governments, business, labour and academic bodies. It is in the interests of all these groups to continue and enlarge the process of co-operation which was begun early in this decade. It is especially in the interest of the federal government for such a western Canada Development Centre to come into being because in the future our confederation will undoubtedly see wider sharing of jurisdiction between Ottawa and the provinces. The west wants not only a marked reduction in interference by the federal government but a shift westward in decision-making on public policy. As the west becomes a stronger component of Canada, our entire country benefits. The improvements in the quality of life which will come about through integrated economic and social planning in the west will benefit surely our whole people. The role of the federal government, then, is to leave the management of those centres to the local people.
The complexity of modern government has often been called a jungle. Here is a way to promote co-operative federalism, at the same time as restoring the belief of people that they can share in creating their own future.

Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Roche) for his very thoughtful and excellent presentation on the subject of his motion before the House today. His speech reflects his very genuine and deep concern for the improvement and betterment of human opportunity in western Canada, as well as elsewhere in the world. His speech was very worth while, although it was somewhat in a different direction than I anticipated when 1 looked at motion No. 12. Perhaps that is a reflection of our experience in this place where we tend to look more at hardware and economic aspects of development.
The debate which is ongoing now as to whether there should be a pipeline and, if so, on what terms, etc., is an important aspect of the development in western Canada, from which flow many of the social problems that were highlighted, pinpointed, ant outlined so clearly in the hon. member's remarks. He touched upon problems common to all prairie provinces, as well as British Columbia. Perhaps these problems are more common to Alberta, and if some of my references stem from
Western Canada Development Centre my somewhat better knowledge of Saskatchewan than Alberta, I am sure the hon. member will understand that.
The hon. member is attempting to provide a format for a human resource development effort which will parallel the natural resource development taking place in the new western Canada. He elaborated by giving a number of specific examples of that. One point which clearly comes to mind with respect to Saskatchewan-and perhaps to a lesser proportion and extent in Alberta and Manitoba-is the growth in the population of Indian, Metis and native people in northern centres all across the northland of the prairies. These people are seeking jobs and economic opportunities on their own home ground. Despite all of the economic activity ongoing in western Canada, the federal and provincial governments have not yet been able to incorporate those people into some of that economic development. There are problems concerning different value systems, traditional lifestyles and so on. All of these things tend to complicate the situation.
Society has tended to resort to the modern day solution of more welfare and more income support, which is not the correct direction. Many of the present day leaders of the native people are very much aware of that fact and are looking to the federal government, provincial agencies and other agencies for the correction of that particular direction. Whether it is through an agency such as that proposed by the hon. member or not, I hope something is achieved.
1 support the objectives and the theme put forward by my hon. friend, although I expected his remarks to relate more to hardware and economic aspects. I am not convinced that the western Canada development centre he proposes is the best route. Having said that, I have no better alternative to offer. I suppose some of my reservations stem from the fact that I have watched both federal and provincial governments for a number of years, and I tend to be a bit cynical when we set up more and more structures, agencies and frameworks. We have many of them in place now, and one problem referred to at the conclusion of my hon. friend's remarks was the problem of a jungle of agencies, whether they be governmental, intergovernmental, private or whatever. The public is confused by the wide variety and scope of agencies. Hence, my concern is whether another major agency covering a broad range of activities and interests would highlight the problems and zero in on them. Would it work fast enough and soon enough? Perhaps an expansion of some of the present agencies would be beneficial.
I recall that the Saskatchewan Research Council at one time was looking very hard at whether it should expand into the social side of things as well as looking at research only from the point of view of economics, pipelines for solids and other topics which had been studied and worked on by both the Alberta and Saskatchewan Research Councils. They were trying to decide whether there should be some mixing of the social problems referred to in this debate. That was explored

February 20, 1978
Western Canada Development Centre
but was not proceeded with, unless that has been done in the last year or so.
As far as the agency being a western Canadian agency is concerned, I support that. As a matter of fact, at the present time the federal government, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), the western premiers and western farm groups are considering the advisability of establishing a prairie rail authority which would handle some of the functions which are now in the hands of the Canadian Transport Commission. In other words, it would bring a better regional flavour and hopefully a better regional appreciation to the problems of rail and railroads in western Canada. If that idea goes forward, there is a precedent in that respect, perhaps not in the same sense that Judge Hall and his commission reported on, but something close to that idea, although expanded somewhat. Here again we have the concept of a former all-federal agency being broken down to look at western Canada alone.
The pipeline debate indicates the very timely nature of this motion. My hon. friend outlined a number of other energy related projects, the magnitude of which is very difficult for most of us here or most Canadians in the west, in the east or in central Canada to comprehend fully. If we are going to proceed with such a centre, I am convinced that it must be a top notch, high calibre institution comprising very capable people who have earned their credentials elsewhere. This is necessary if their work or pronouncements are to have any real effect. Anything less would be of no real value. We have had enough ministerial committees, subcommittees, ad hoc committees and so forth. Some of that is necessary on a time to time basis, there is no question about that; but if this agency is to do the job my hon. friend holds out for it-and I share his objectives-it has to be an agency with some real statute. Of course, that will not happen overnight. That will take some time to develop, but I suppose a beginning must be made somewhere.
Perhaps there is a lack of private, independent spokesmen or agencies in the social field. We can look to the Science Council of Canada, to the Economic Council of Canada, or to the Conference Board. There are a number of agencies in the economic field, but there is not a long list of primarily social agencies, at least any which have any tremendous clout. There are federal energy regulatory bodies, provincial energy regulatory bodies and so forth. As everyone recognizes, the track record of those bodies with regard to energy supplies over the last few years has certainly not been good. The entire energy picture in this country was clouded, first of all, by the OPEC cartel of several years ago which brought about dramatic increases in prices which, in turn, brought about bickering and fighting between the federal and provincial governments about who should get all or most of the tax revenues from the various resource companies. That has tended to cloud the whole question of energy development in the country over the last few years.
Again I compliment the hon. member for raising the social side of the whole question. As far as western regional matters are concerned, I think we have done not too badly. We can

look back to the PFRA of the 1930s. We can look to the Prairie Economic Council of 1965. I was with the provincial government of Saskatchewan when the first meeting was held. It was interesting to see premiers of diverse political views at that time-and that has not changed very much since- continuing that work and that liaison. We can look to what has resulted from those beginnings. We now see the premiers of the prairie provinces getting together. The PFRA and the concerted efforts of those years were seen again last year when it did not take the various governments and federal authorities very long to zero in on the 1977 drought threat which faced many parts of western Canada. The machinery was there. Work experience and the idea of getting together to tackle problems were not new to anyone.
Another agency which has come along but perhaps has not yet zeroed in on the social side of development in western Canada or, indeed, elsewhere in Canada, is the federal Department of Regional Economic Expansion which, as hon. members know, was set up in 1969. DREE has zeroed in on specific industrial enterprises and assistance in terms of job creation. It has gone a considerable distance. The general development agreement is now signed with each province. We can go from there and point out specific things, such as a coal agreement with respect to British Columbia and a steel agreement related to Saskatchewan. The development of Ipsco has been timely because that company is now in a position, if there is further expansion, to take advantage of some of the opportunities which will be coming to western Canada if the pipeline project is proceeded with. That is another example of federal-provincial co-operation. It is the result of effort and study on the part not only of provincial and federal governments but also of other groups and agencies located in the prairie provinces. I think we should give some credit to officials in the Department of Regional Economic Expansion for developments in this area in recent years.
[DOT] (W42)
My hon. friend referred to the conference that took place in Lethbridge. I believe the mere fact that people came together and discussed the various subjects that came up without concern about provincial rights and so forth is a good omen. The Western Economic Opportunities Conference was mentioned as well. That was also the product of hard work and effort on the part of everyone concerned. Of course, like the conference that took place just last week, it could be called either a success or a failure, but I believe the WEOC which took place in Calgary in 1973 was a good beginning. A number of good things came out of that conference and action is being taken in many areas, such as transportation, agriculture and the western Canada northland agreement in the three provinces. These are what we might call "hardware" programs even though some are related to energy. But they create a climate for co-operation.
I should like to turn to my personal concern about whether an agency of the type suggested by my hon. friend will ever be established. I think we need to hear from the provincial governments and their agencies as well as the Canada West

Foundation as to whether they support this concept or would rather expand existing machinery. I cannot help but be a little concerned about establishing a sort of blanket agency. I think something with clear-cut objectives would have more chance of success. I support the concept in principle, however, although I think it needs further consideration about whether it is the correct route to follow. I commend the hon. member for bringing the motion forward and I hope the idea can be pursued not only in this House but in other fora.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED DATA COLLECTION AND MONITORING AGENCY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is a sense in which the debate this afternoon is typical of the kinds of debates we have in private members' hour. The hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Roche), a member of the opposition, has put forward an excellent idea and backed it with a very effective speech. The hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley (Mr. Mclsaac), a member for the government, has found no course but to agree with the ideas put forward. In fact, his speech was also a very good one in which he strengthened the case; but in the end he says he is not sure that we should let the motion pass because, in his view, it sets up another body or agency. I suppose that means that my hon. friend from Edmonton-Strathcona will get praise for the rest of the afternoon but that at six o'clock the motion will not be passed; it will be talked out.
Not only do I think the motion is a good one and that the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona made an excellent speech, but I believe the House ought to pass the motion this afternoon. I emphasize that even if it were passed it would not set up the development centre. All it would do is to express the opinion of the House. It would be up to the government whether it acted on that opinion.
As for the criticisms from across the way to the effect that the motion seemed to talk too much in terms of hardware, I emphasize that the gist of the motion was to have an institute that would be concerned about policies to ensure integrated, economic and social development in western Canada. The whole proposal is concerned with the quality of life as opposed to the hardware that dominates the way we live.
I am reminded of the debate we had seven days ago on the motion presented by the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker)-one that used to be presented from time to time by the former member for Malpeque, Angus MacLean. In that case, he was concerned about a certain aspect of life, namely the environment; he was concerned because of what it does to the quality of life.
This afternoon the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona is likewise concerned about the quality of life. I thought his dissertation was first rate when he tried to find a balance between the material and the spiritual, between whether we should try to get individuals to become perfect or reform society to make it possible for us to become individuals. I subscribe to the philosophy he presented. If I might be so presumptuous as to sum up what he said, he was saying that man cannot live by bread alone, but man cannot live at all if there is no bread, and perhaps there has to be a quite a bit of bread if we are to have the kind of life that is possible today.
Western Canada Development Centre
As the hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley pointed out, there are plenty of agencies that deal with so-called hardware matters-the Economic Council of Canada, the Conference Board in Canada and various research bodies. The country is full of them. But there are not very many instances where studies are made, under government auspices, of what our economic development is doing to the quality of life of human beings in this country.
I belong to a generation that long ago was deeply concerned about the indignities human beings were suffering because economics went completely haywire. I think I can say for that generation that in our younger days we were determined not only to solve the economic problems but to build the kind of Canada in which human beings would not suffer the terrible indignities and heartbreaks that we went through in a decade, four or five decades ago.
I believe that today, even with the greater affluence that is around, mixed as it is with unemployment, there is a subconscious realization that we have to build not only railroads, pipelines, transportation and all the rest, but also a real quality of life. It would not hurt us in this House this afternoon to pass a motion saying that, in our view, the government ought to consider setting up a western Canada development centre to be concerned about the quality of life in this new and growing part of the country. I am pleased with the speech my hon. friend made this afternoon. I support his motion.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my remarks will be brief because, like the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), I should like to see this motion come to a vote and pass. All three parties have expressed the opinion that this is a very reasoned and responsible motion, with a well thought out and researched speech delivered by the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Roche).
It would be appropriate for me to try to qualify what are a couple of misconceptions put forward by the hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley (Mr. Mclsaac). I want to commend him because his reply to the motion was responsible comment and his reasoning was one that we on this side of the House would want to applaud. He said that one of the things in this country which we do not need is a proliferation of agencies; that is not a direct quote but the gist of his remarks. It is also the mutual feeling of the majority of members in this House.
There is a misunderstanding of what the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona is trying to propose in motion No. 12 today. First of all, he is asking the government to give consideration to establishing such an agency, which would be an all encompassing group, but in essence its input would be from the grassroots and from the conferences the agency would hold throughout the provinces. In other words, it is not an attempt to establish something that is bureaucratic in nature, but rather is information collection for recommendation to governments at all three levels.

February 20, 1978
Western Canada Development Centre
Because that is the principle, we are not looking at something we can really refer to as being of bureaucratic nature. It is not an attempt to establish some new branch or department of the government. It is not an attempt to develop a several tiered bureaucracy. It is simply a case of trying to establish an agency which sets up a mode of communication through which the people of western Canada can touch bases with governments at all levels.
I have several pages of notes, but I do not want to delay a vote on this issue. I just want to illustrate one example of the importance of what the member for Edmonton-Strathcona has been saying. We have talked about the pipeline labour pressure. We predict they will be there with the pipeline coming from Alaska, the Yukon and the province of Alberta and with it its accompanying influx of labour. Fort McMurray is a town in the province of Alberta. Fort McMurray is a wealthy town with a lot of money per capita. There is a very high ratio of males over females. It is also a place no one really calls home. In the supermarkets, stores and hotels of Fort McMurray, people when they meet and greet each other ask: "Where are you from?" The answer will be that they are from Oklahoma, Texas, Ontario, and so on. They are not from Fort McMurray. Many of these people have lived there five, six and 10 years, but they do not think of it as home. The result is a community with a lot of money, and unbalanced sex ratio and a high crime rate. It houses one of the busiest police forces in Alberta. That is one example of an economic boom taking place without concern for the social stress that it will cause for a community.
I would like to conclude by asking that all members of this House cease speaking at this time and let come to a vote a very worthy and justifiable motion, one that should receive the consideration of this House.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment

Mr. Speaker, I would also like to compliment the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Roche) for the second point which he stressed in his dissertation, that being the quality of life. Many of us in this House do not consider that question as much as we should. I congratulate him for his continuing interest in an area which I consider important.
Someone said to me a short while ago: "There is an interesting situation that is happening in this world, Mr. Anderson. We have aircraft which can fly at twice the speed of sound. One can fly from Paris to New York in four hours and save five or six hours in travelling time. What is the point in getting there that fast if when you arrive you have no purpose in being there early?" In other words, we have developed a society where technology perhaps has outpaced our values in life. As a result, some things happen in society as a result of our not paying attention to the quality of life which the hon. member has stressed.
I agree with the comment which the hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley (Mr. Mclsaac) made that there has been a long history of co-operation in western Canada. There has had to be, I suppose. It was the situation of necessity being the mother of invention. It is also true that the west has not

had the same amount of economic clout and attention which central Canada has had for a number of years. I can understand why that economic clout has not been there. The day is coming where the centre of gravity in this country will move to the west. The potential of the west is being realized. The hon. member is right in pointing out that as a shift occurs there must be more attention paid to the area which has not received the same amount of attention from various groups-the Economic Council of Canada, for instance.
In the province of British Columbia we have a grassroots situation where regional districts are being funded by DREE. Economic advisers are paid for by the federal government so that at the regional level as well as at the municipal and city level there are people making decisions in small communities which are appropriate only to their own area. Councils, regional districts, municipalities, provinces and the federal government are all becoming involved in a variety of economic chores and economic decisions which each one has to make in its own sphere of activity. At this point is it wise to bring in a further group?
I am not speaking against this suggestion, but I am saying we have these groups established at the present time. Should we have another body involved in economic decisions in western Canada? The hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona realizes the difficulty we have in getting provinces to agree with the federal government. We are aware also of the sometimes confrontation situation that exists between provincial and municipal governments. And now, in the case of British Columbia, we have regional districts, which is another form of government.
1 wonder if, in view of the good intentions of the proposals in the motion the hon. member has put forward, he has a solution-

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF AGENCY TO SUPERVISE PIPELINE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in my earlier remarks on Bill C-25, I referred to the Lysyk report. I asked questions regarding the second stage inquiry. Evidently we are not going to get this. The second study to be conducted by the pipeline monitoring agency is not the type of second stage inquiry that the Canadian people, specifically those in the Yukon, were promised.
The second question I asked was what had happened to the strong, unanimous recommendation that, in order to avoid prejudice to a just settlement of the Yukon Indian land claims, pipeline construction should not proceed before August 1, 1981. If those in the government and the people to my right have their way, construction will begin prior to that. Indeed, judging from their remarks, many of those to my right would like to see the building of that pipeline start tomorrow morning. Settlement of the land claims will not be accorded the priority and urgency they deserve.
Third, what happened to the $200 million heritage fund which was recommended by the National Energy Board? We did not get that. Instead, the people in the Yukon got the right to borrow up to $200 million. They will have to pay interest on that loan. I do not know what the people in the Yukon can expect other than, as I mentioned earlier, the building of this pipeline through their territory and not too much good along with it.
There is provision in the legislation for the establishment of an agency to monitor construction of the pipeline. Such an agency was called for by the Lysyk inquiry and by the leader of my party when we supported the Alcan proposal in principle last August. At that time we demanded as much public input and scrutiny over the project as possible. However, the monitoring agency which this bill proposes is not at all what we had in mind.
What we will get is another government body responsible to a minister. We will get a group of bureaucrats in Ottawa & Calgary who will operate beyond the scrutiny of parliament. What we will have is a very powerful instrument in the hands of the government, with a very limited appeal procedure which stops at the Federal Court.
Northern Pipeline
What is missing from this legislation is far more important than what is included. We do not have the grassroots participation of those in the Yukon in the monitoring agency. We do not have massive participation on the part of the Yukon people or on the part of people along the route of this pipeline.
There is no public involvement in the establishment of the conditions and terms of this agency. Instead, there is token participation on the advisory council. I am afraid as much attention will be paid to the advisory council as was paid to the recommendations of the Lysyk inquiry. I ask: How is this agency going to protect the rights of Yukoners? What steps will be taken to prevent environmental damage? How will the agency be staffed?
Will the government appoint as commissioner a person who has good understanding of the northern people and of the land of the north as well as having proven administrative capabilities? I think, for example, of Mr. Stewart Hodgson who is presently Commissioner of the Northwest Territories. I believe the government should have a talk with him and find out whether he would agree to take this position. If he did, it would create a vacancy in the administration of the Northwest Territories. The government could then move to bring in legislation whereby the position of Commissioner would be up for election. This would mean a greater degree of autonomy for the Northwest Territories. If the present Commissioner would like to head up this monitoring agency, I think he would do a good job.
What of native claims? The legislation makes no mention of them. During the debate in the Commons on August 4 and 5 last, concerning a northern gas pipeline, my party moved an amendment to the motion before the House as follows:
That no pipeline construction precede a fair settlement of native land claims.
That is still our position. As things stand, the Yukon Indians are being asked to negotiate under duress. I would draw your attention, Mr. Speaker, to a statement made by the United States secretary for energy on September 23, 1977:
The Canadian government has made a clear public statement that settlement of native claims in the Yukon will neither delay the project nor increase costs.
I need not repeat the recommendation of the Lysyk inquiry with regard to native claims. As recently as January 25 of this year I sought to move under the provisions of Standing Order
43:
That this House is of the opinion that the government should begin negotiations immediately with a view to settling the land claims of the Yukon native Indians in principle prior to the commencement of the construction of the proposed northern pipeline.
Again I strongly urge the government to reach a settlement in principle with the Yukon Indians as soon as possible. This should be done not only quickly but efficiently and to the satisfaction of all parties. I cannot help thinking of the recent first ministers' conference which was held here in Ottawa recently. Although major topics were under discussion, northerners were not represented at the conference. The government continues to treat the northern territories as colonies to use as

Ottawa sees fit. The elected councillors in the Yukon and in the Territories are not treated by the government as governments but as an administrative extension of the federal department concerned. This is not satisfactory to the people who live in the north.
Finally, since the government and hon. members to my right are determined to build this pipeline regardless of the adverse effects the project will have on the Yukon, I can only say that the bill in its present form is a shameful piece of legislation. The long term effects will be seen in the years to come and I am not at all sure they will be anything to be proud of. Surely, legislation could be brought down which would be responsive to the concerns and needs of northerners. My hon. friends and I will continue to speak out on their behalf.
Has the government really thought about the way in which the lives of the people in the north will be affected by the Alcan project? There are a number of guarantees which should have been written into this bill. My leader has been talking about one of them across the country for months. I refer to a guarantee of jobs. Guarantees should have been written into the legislation ensuring first priority for the people of the north-and here I am talking not only of the population of the Yukon but of those who live along the Mackenzie Valley. Arrangements should have been made for the shuttling of workers between the Mackenzie, the Western Arctic, the Arctic in general and the Yukon. Travel facilities should be upgraded. Improvements should be made at a number of airports. We need more VOR's as soon as possible to improve the safety of navigation, particularly one at Mayo and another at Fort McPherson. Also, I think it is necessary that the Alaska Highway be paved. The United States should be asked to defray a good deal of this expense because Alaskans make a lot more use of the highway than does the Canadian public. The highway will be used very heavily during the construction of the pipeline.

With regard to the speech made in the House by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas), my only regret is that I was not present in the House to hear it. I would call it one of those terrific speeches of which the hon. member has been capable during his long career in politics in the last 40 or so years. He was at his best in that speech. He
February 20, 1978

lamented the fact that we in Canada were the little guys, that those terrible Americans, our enemies, were the big guys and there was no way we could make a deal which would benefit us, the little guys. If they were hard bargainers, he said, then you would know because they would have stolen your shirt, or something like that. It was a typical speech of the kind he used to make in his early days in Saskatchewan when he was premier of that province. He continues to be afraid of development, fearful of being the small participant who might eventually be robbed by the big guy.
His party speaks of creating jobs. No other province in Canada lost more jobs than Saskatchewan when the hon. member was premier of that province in the early days of his premiership. They left in droves. I cannot believe he was particularly concerned about jobs at that time. Nor does he seem to be concerned about them now. He is still, as he was in those days, a tremendously entertaining speaker, a very concerned member, but has little confidence in Canada and Canadians and in our ability to deal with those who may appear to be bigger than we are.
I read the speech of the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. Holmes) with regard to native claims. I looked through it carefully in search of his solution to that difficult problem, but I failed to find it. He dealt with the subject but failed to come up with a solution. It is easy to complain about a problem. It is far more difficult to find a solution to it. I admit the problem is a difficult one.
Last but not least I come to the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent). He has been crying out in the House for jobs, more jobs, yet his party cannot even say whether or not they are in favour of the pipeline agreement. The NDP must make up its mind. The hon. member has tried his utmost to create a climate of insecurity and instability with regard to the building of the pipeline. Moreover, the anti-dumping option would really only come into play after the fact, which renders its use, other than as a threat mechanism, somewhat ineffective.
Let me say too that the northern gas pipeline project is primarily intended to deliver gas to U.S. customers. Therefore, there should be little or no subsidization of U.S. consumers through the mechanism of financing the construction of the pipeline. It is not in the interests of the Canadian and U.S. governments to subsidize their own consumers in respect of energy costs at a time when it is the policy of both governments to emphasize energy conservation and discourage energy use wherever possible. For the United States to provide concessional financing through the Export Import Bank on the grounds that the transit pipeline is in another country would be contrary to the policy objective.
The main section of the northern gas pipeline to be built in Canada is being designed to accommodate-this was spoken about before and I am attempting to cover those things which were not covered as yet-2.4 Bcf of Alaskan gas and 1.2 Bcf of Canadian gas to the southern markets. The Prudhoe Bay supply will represent approximately 5 per cent of U.S. consumption. Canada is currently producing about 8.5 Bcfs a day of natural gas, 2.7 BcFs of which are exported to the United States.

By their actions the Liberals have dangerously delayed this bill, and I want to emphasize "dangerously". The Liberals have risked the destiny of Canada with the political game they have been playing and with what I submit they have been attempting to do with this bill. Northern Pipeline
attempt to get answers, debate it long enough that there would be a risk of losing the pipeline.
I submit that the Liberals might play that kind of politics in the hope of demonstrating to the people of Canada that we on this side killed the bill. We have news for them. The Progressive Conservative party demands that the bill include effective monitoring capability of the proposed pipeline agency by parliament so that the Canadian content requirement might be met. Before I conclude I should like to comment on some aspects of the Alaska Highway. The Liberal government has been derelict in its duty in regard to this highway and has shown a miserable lack of vision when it comes to the north and its resources.
The Alaska Highway was built in nine months in 1942. For years Canada was blind to the potential of the north and failed to recognize the potential to the economy of resources and

tourism in that part of the country. It was a former government under the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) that built the "roads to resources" and started paving sections of the Alaska Highway. A former Prime Minister, Mr. Pearson, referred to that program as the government spending money in the Yukon like a drunken sailor- "building highways from igloo to igloo." That was being short-sighted, Mr. Speaker. Today, we have a major highway there and plans for a major pipeline. Before the highway is paved there will undoubtedly be changes in its route.
Pipe will not be laid in the Yukon before 1981. Meantime the government should study the highway in the Yukon immediately and consider its route before it is all paved. It does not make sense for a pipeline to dictate where the highway should go, nor does it make sense for them not to run parallel. Had the previous plan been followed, the Alaska Highway would be paved today; but as it is not, there is still time to survey and reroute it if it is considered necessary.
For the information of this government, Mr. Speaker, tourism makes money. Our present tourism deficit is approximately $2 billion but we could attract many American tourists were it not for that dusty, rocky road. A paved road through the Yukon would bring many more American dollars to this country.
There are others in my party who want to speak this evening. I conclude by emphasizing that the pipeline should be an investment opportunity for all Canadians. I believe in the concept of equity participation. An example of this is Alberta Gas Trunk Line, in which the people of Alberta were allowed to buy shares. We do not need another Crown corporation; this government already have so many that they cannot count them all. The people should be allowed to participate in a venture like this by subscribing for shares. When Alberta Gas Trunk Line put their shares on the market they were soon oversubscribed.
I note the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce is still talking quite a bit. He may want a seance with Mackenzie King. I would like to give one more quote to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. I note tonight there is a significant change in his position. On September 20, 1977 in a press interview with the Calgary Herald he said that-
-his department will ensure Canadian companies have the inside track on bidding, as well as insisting on a high degree of Canadian content in the manufactured goods used on the project. . . intends to play an integral role-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is a chap on the other side who shoots from the lip far too fast. I have spent some time in the trenches laying pipe in this country, whether it be water or services piping, and I know what it is like to be in the trenches and to work outside in temperatures at eight or 10 degrees below zero.
In this debate on the pipeline issue there are those on the other side of the House who have been saying for so long there is too much control, too much government intervention in the lives of people in this country. To me that is ironic. For suddenly the NDP are saying: "Come on, government, you must guarantee our workers these jobs and you must guarantee a certain amount of Canadian content. You must reach into our lives and pocketbooks and guarantee our livelihood for us". I find it strange that people who, on certain days of the week, do not want controls, on other days, when we debate the pipeline, such as today, do want controls, guarantees and everything else handed to them.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF AGENCY TO SUPERVISE PIPELINE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext: We want jobs for Canadians.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF AGENCY TO SUPERVISE PIPELINE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
We are all interested in jobs for Canadians, Mr. Speaker. To those who spend so much time badgering for job guarantees for Canadians, I say I have yet to hear them talk about the ultimate cost to Canada if it was to provide those guarantees, what it would amount to in terms of contracts to be signed as well as involvement in the livelihoods of Canadians. Even those with the least amount of common sense in this House, looking at the question of guaranteeing work, putting an absolute guarantee on these jobs and on content, would see that the first thing that would happen is that the lid would blow off the cost of the pipeline. The moment a guarantee
Northern Pipeline
went into the jobs, the content or whatever, you could well expect that the cost would substantially escalate. Everyone would want to grab the biggest piece of the pie that they could. There would be no control left. How long would it be before the cost of that pipeline would double or triple?
The government has said to workers and to companies in this country: "There is every opportunity for you to obtain work on this pipeline, there is every opportunity for you to supply Canadian goods which go into the building of the pipeline and there is every opportunity for Canadians to come off the unemployment rolls and secure jobs in building the pipeline or making parts for it. But to do that you must stay competitive."
This pipeline is not only important to this country between now and 1982, 1983 or 1984. What will happen to our economy when the pipeline is completed and when we begin to ship the oil and gas? We have to have a sound economy, and we cannot continue to do so if, during the course of building the pipeline, wage rates, the cost of equipment, goods and so on completely skyrocket and get out of line. This will destroy the prosperity not only of people who work on the pipeline or who make products for it, but the rest of the economy as well, because so much of our economy is fed by the energy which is delivered to run plants that produce other products.
All of us in this House have a common interest in Canadian plants doing work and in Canadian workers getting jobs to build a pipeline. Everyone is I am sure very hopeful that the maximum benefits to Canada will result from the building of the pipeline. It is a joint project between two countries, and when you have a situation like that no one country can expect it to go all one way. I have a lot of confidence in what the Canadian worker can do on the pipeline and what good Canadians can produce for the pipeline. When I look at the cost of the pipeline and see that two-thirds is taken up in building the United States portion and about one-third in building the Canadian portion, I would like to think that Canadians could be competitive enough, and are competitive enough, not only to bid for, build and work on the pipeline in Canada, but that they will be able to look forward to bidding for, building and working on a portion in the United States as well.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would appreciate its being asked at the end of my remarks, if the hon. member would allow me two or three more minutes.
We have a good deal in this pipeline. If we manage to stay competitive and manage to build the Canadian section of the pipeline with no more than 35 per cent cost overrun beyond

February 20, 1978
Northern Pipeline
our present projections, we will virtually have the Canadian side built and maintained for nothing. That is a good deal for this country and a compliment to the hon. House leader who negotiated the arrangement. We also receive an insurance protection fund for the Yukon and the northern territories which is far greater than what Dean Lysyk expected would be coming forward.
It is important that the Canadian people understand one thing. The gas Canadians will eventually receive via the pipeline once the Canadian section is built will be twice as important to us as the gas which will be shipped to the Americans in the lower 48 states.
I am afraid I am competing against the rest of the House. I beg their indulgence for about two minutes. That gas being shipped through the pipeline to the United States will be sufficient to serve 5 per cent of their energy requirements. Canadian gas shipped through that pipeline to the Canadian market will supply 10 per cent of Canadian energy requirements. Therefore, the gas going through the pipeline will be twice as important to us as that going to the United States. If our costs go up through the building of that pipeline as a result of letting them get out of control and not remaining competitive, the ultimate effect will reflect twice as hard upon the Canadian economy as the American economy. That is something we cannot stand and do not need.
I will sum up by asking a few short questions of my friends from the New Democratic Party. For weeks they have been saying there must be a flat-out guarantee of jobs for Canadians, of Canadian content going into the building of the Canadian pipeline, and of Canadian workers being employed. Has anyone yet heard the leader of the NDP or one of his spokesmen offer corresponding guarantees in return, not just to this House, but to the Canadian people? They are asking for guaranteed jobs for Canadians and a guarantee that Canadian pipe will go into the pipeline. Has anyone from the NDP yet said to the Canadian people they will guarantee workmanship going into the pipe? Has anyone yet said that they will guarantee to keep the cost of the pipe down, guarantee delivery on time and guarantee workmanship? I have not yet heard one guarantee corresponding to the guarantee for which they ask.
Not one of us would hire a doctor, plumber, lawyer or any artisan to do work for us, saying that we will give him a blanket guarantee, without asking in return for a guarantee of workmanship, quality and delivery. We would also like to be assured that workers will not go out on strike, so that the job will be done on time. No one in the NDP has offered a guarantee like that in return for the guarantee for which they are asking. The best guarantee, the best way to achieve that, is to leave it up to the free enterprise system. When you have people competing for the jobs, wages and the products going into the pipeline, the best result comes from allowing the free marketplace to prevail.

I agree it is necessary to put on controls so that the Canadian competitor has a fair and equitable chance. We do that by setting up the control and review agency as expounded by the House leader. That is the guarantee of control. It ensures that Canadians get a fair deal in this pipeline project.
I find it strange that our friends in the NDP who purport to act for the little guy, who represent the workers of this country, have less faith in the ability of the Canadian workman, less confidence in his competence and desire to do a job, than the president of the steel company. I find that very strange.
I said I would be short, Mr. Speaker.

How can he reconcile what he calls a good, healthy, free competitive market for pipeline material, which in turn means jobs for Canadians, when steel companies in Japan, West Germany, Italy, and indeed the United States through DISC, have decided advantages and in some cases are very heavily subsidized by taxpayers through government aid? If he can say that our steel companies are in the same competitive position as those in Japan, West Germany, Italy and the United States, I will accept his argument. I want him to substantiate his charge that it would be a free competitive-
