Mr. Speaker, during the course of my remarks I stated that I believe the Canadian steel industry is competitive. I believe Canadian workers can do the job. The companies can turn out the products, whether it be Stelco, Ipsco, or the myriad of smaller companies that will in fact be making parts that go into the pipeline. I believe they are competitive.
In my remarks I stated that it is essential to create a situation where the free enterprise system would prevail. We must ensure that everyone remains competitive and that Canadians remain just as competitive for the long run improvements in our economy as the short run improvements. I also said that I am not naive about what goes on in the world, that there is international commerce, trade and competition and that it is necessary to have a control mechanism, a watchdog body or review agency. We have in terms of the legislation set one up which can look at the bids as they come in. It will ensure that Canadians get a fair chance to bid competitively and equitably on the materials that go into the pipeline; that is set up by the control mechanism. Since the
February 20, 1978

permits given are conditional on the proposal made and the proposal says we are trying to reach at least 90 per cent Canadian content, we will watch the progress in that regard. We will ensure the companies do their utmost to do that. We will ensure they are not faced with unfair competition.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF AGENCY TO SUPERVISE PIPELINE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my speech tonight is on how to make money. I have listened to some very fine speeches in the House, all dealing with the amount of Canadian content, the man working in the steel mill, the man who makes the valves, pumps and so on in Quebec or the Atlantic provinces. That is all good material to be talking about. However, for too long this House has forgotten the main objective that this pipeline gives us.
As I said in August, I speak with great sadness on this subject because never has there been a crime committed against the Canadian people greater than the crime that the Liberal party of this country has committed on the subject of pipelines over the past 25 years.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF AGENCY TO SUPERVISE PIPELINE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF AGENCY TO SUPERVISE PIPELINE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
I am old
enough to remember, as is the House leader, that when Canadian companies tried to build a pipeline from the Peace River in British Columbia to service Canadians who lived in the city of Vancouver and needed a few extra thousand cubic feet of market to make that pipeline a paying proposition, they got that market. They got it because El Paso came in from the United States and said: We will buy that extra 200,000 cubic feet if you will give it to us for 50 per cent less than Canadians pay for it. The men who formed this company took all the risks of building that pipeline through high mountains-the highest mountains a pipeline has ever been built through-and did it without any protection from the government of Canada. Before they could get that extra sale they had to accept a price of 22 cents a thousand when Canadians closer to the source had to pay 33 cents.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF AGENCY TO SUPERVISE PIPELINE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext: Shame!

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF AGENCY TO SUPERVISE PIPELINE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
Moreover, the Liberal government of that day sat here and did nothing when that same American company asked for 50 per cent of the shares in addition as a sweetener to the low price they were paying. It finally got 25 per cent. So great was the outrage among those of us who were beginning to take an interest in these matters at that time that an attack began to develop on the federal Liberals, culminating in the debates surrounding the trans-Canada pipeline which was the Liberals' next great hurdle.
The head of the Department of Trade and Commerce at that time believed that Canadians were not competent to finance a pipeline or to build a pipeline or even to run a pipeline. And almost all of the trans-Canada pipeline, which ran from the border of Alberta and Saskatchewan right down to the heartland of our industry in Toronto and Montreal, was
Northern Pipeline
built; not only with American financing by way of bonds but with American equity money. Finally, toward the end of that campaign, to get the government to speak up for Canada and Canadians they finally allowed Canadian citizens to buy a few million dollars worth of equity. If you bought a $100 bond they would let you buy five shares at $10 apiece. The issue was oversubscribed many times; we never even found out by how much we had oversubscribed it. These are memories of the sell-out of the Canadian people to the Texas buccaneers by those who sat on the other side of the House in 1956.

speechtext: That includes you Allan!

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF AGENCY TO SUPERVISE PIPELINE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext: 1 was so far away on the backbenches you couldn't even see me.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF AGENCY TO SUPERVISE PIPELINE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
When I heard the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) stand up and read a statement prepared by people who had given him a lot of figures to quote, it was hard to realize that the minister comes from a proud political family, a family proud of its services to this country, proud of being devoted to principles for which they have always fought. Better the hon. gentleman should have been back out in Crowfoot trying to save himself than be associated with a group of people like those around him now on an issue such as this. I felt very sorry for him. I felt very sorry for his family which for four generations has fought for the fundamental principles which have put this country together. I was sorry he had to make a speech like that. And all he could do, with the name-calling which went on across the House, was to lose his temper. I do not blame him, thinking, as he must, of all the men who have gone before him and carried his name. Birds of a feather must flock together. The "same old bunch" all over again.
This bill, as has been explained by the minister, carries out, in effect, one of the duties of the National Energy Board, namely, to give a certificate of convenience and public necessity to this pipeline. It has been made very clear to us that primarily we are talking about a pipeline of convenience intended to move American gas to Americans. It is true that a few cubic feet will be supplied to towns in Canada along the route of the line. We are doing this as a good neighbour should to provide a convenience for our American friends. They were ready to assist us, too. In 1966, just 12 years ago, we wanted to build a loop in our major pipeline across from Manitoba into Ontario passing through their territory. We got a pipeline through there. But notice what they did: they asked for and got, as they thought was their due, 50 per cent of the equity. This brings me around full circle to where we stand tonight.
This bill suffers from the fact that it was not brought in last fall when it should have been brought in. Had that timetable been followed, we could have used the power of this House by putting in one or two conditions which would have helped this Canadian consortium composed of Westcoast Transmission and Alberta Gas Trunk. This consortium could have used some help. The Canadian portion of the line was going to cost less than $4 billion. To many people this looked like a big

February 20, 1978
Northern Pipeline
project. But Canadians can carry it without too much sweat if we pull together. We could have helped this Canadian company to get the necessary financing if we had done certain things for which there is a precedent.
During this debate almost every speaker for the official opposition has mentioned the technique-that is, equity. A great majority of people, I am afraid, do not understand the significance of equity when it comes to pipeline financing. I think it can be best understood if one realizes that the people who put up the equity must wait for a return on their money; the first charge on the earnings of a pipeline company goes to pay off bond holders. We have in place, thanks to the government of my right hon. friend from Prince Albert (Mr. Diefen-baker), the National Energy Board Act of 1959 which provides that in future a National Energy Board shall lay down conditions which ensure that a private company operating a pipeline is working in the interests of Canada-and those interests include many things, among them financing.
Where do we find in this bill any mention of conditions laid down with regard to the financing of the pipeline to make sure that Canadian content where it really counts-ownership- will be protected? There is nothing of that kind in the legislation. It never crossed the minds of members sitting on the treasury benches opposite, those great minds still living in awe of C. D. Howe who thought Canadians were not brainy enough, not gutsy enough, not sufficiently well financed to build a pipeline. This group of people opposite, this crowd of nitwits, are surrounded by experts who know nothing about anything, as we saw tonight by that speech given by the minister.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF AGENCY TO SUPERVISE PIPELINE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext: Experts anonymous!

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF AGENCY TO SUPERVISE PIPELINE CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
The Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, had it known what it should know-because at one time pipelines were within its jurisdiction-should have provided the minister with a series of speeches setting out all that had been done during the negotiations with the Americans and with the private companies to show, above all, that they were backing up this Canadian company and securing for Canadians the first opportunity to finance it.
I do not intend to examine the whole of the financial structure of Westcoast or Trans-Canada Pipeline or Great Lakes in detail. I have lived through the events connected with each one of them. Now I am living through the fourth one. And when I see a government which has not learned from these mistakes, when we have to work with a government which has no shame, a government which will not take advantage of the possibilities open to it, I can only shake my head. The real value of a pipeline is not in hardware. It lies with the person who owns it. It lies with ownership of the equity shares.
The Conservative party from time immemorial has been the only party which clearly states that our objective is to have Canadians as individuals owning this country.
I congratulate the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas). Thank goodness that, with all his

experience and knowledge, he had enough brains to come to the House and say he supports this equity approach, that he does not support doctrinaire socialism, not when it comes to his country. He gave his promise in 1953 in Saskatchewan as a premier that so long as he was premier he would see to it that the oil and gas companies, which had promised to develop that province, would never be nationalized or socialized. He has lived long enough to see doctrinaire socialists break his word. He has seen how Saskatchewan has been put on its back. But here he stood up and said that equity is worthwhile.
He supported the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Neilsen) who said that we must have some parliamentary control, not so much over the companies but over this crowd of people who have a record of 25 years of selling out the Canadian people at every opportunity they get. There has been no greater demonstration of this than in the pipeline fiasco over the last 25 years.
Fortunately for this country the National Energy Board Act is in place. Fortunately for this country, even though the National Energy Board has been emasculated by the officials of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce who have not given the board an opportunity to carry out its full functions, the board is still there, even though it has been pushed around and interfered with by this government. When the board sets its rate of return on the rate base for this pipeline for the partners in Canada, it will make certain that the rate of return on equity is based on the full amount of money borrowed plus the amount of equity. That is called the rate base. So the money that equity gets, if they want to get more money, depends on the size of the rate base.
It is true that the National Energy Board over the years has assumed that when the pipeline is built and is operated it will not be a risky enterprise but a success, and they do not give a rate of return that is as high as it used to be when interest rates were 6 per cent. I am simply pointing out that sooner or later the National Energy Board will discover what is the true function of setting the rate of return, namely, some relationship to competitive risk costs around the world. Today if you want to know what risk money draws, you should go and look at countries such as the United Kingdom. They have been developing the North Sea fields at great speed, which got them off the economic hook. What rate of return did that socialist government in name offer to private industry to develop the North Sea oil? They offered approximately 25 per cent on the rate base.
The effective rate base we have in Canada, on the basis of most decisions I have seen, is around 14 per cent or 15 per cent. Sooner or later that rate of return has to match the rate of return in other countries. I am simply saying that the only chance Canadians have-whether they live on a farm, work in a factory or work at any other white collar or blue collar job, apart from steel workers, construction workers and a few others-to make any money out of this is if an opportunity is provided them to buy that equity.
February 20, 1978

The companies that I have mentioned, such as Westcoast and Alberta Gas Trunk, are both Canadian. They know what I am talking about because one of them was gored in 1954 and the other happened to have a government in charge in Alberta which put in statutory terms what we should have in front of us here. Sure enough, the statute of 1954 was replaced. I may mention a few of the changes later, but now I will ask members on the government side to follow the precedent set by the government of Alberta, composed of a mixture of farmers, professional people and average folk such as we have in this House. I should like to read a clause from chapter 37 of the 1954 statutes. It reads:
Capitalization
5. The capital stock of the company shall consist of
(a)	eight million Class "A" common shares of the par value of five dollars with no voting rights attached to the shares, and
(b)	two thousand and two Class "B" common shares of the par value of five dollars with voting rights attached to the shares.
The ordinary people of Alberta were authorized under this statute to acquire eight million common shares at $5 apiece. All the big companies that were out finding the oil or gas, distributing it and selling it, were allowed 2,000 shares, and the act specifically allocated the number of shares to each class.
People who were expert in financing in those days said the Canadians were not able to finance a pipeline. I happened to be in Alberta on that day, as were a large number of Saskatchewan residents, all of us trying to pass ourselves off as Albertan residents to get access to these common shares. Because the regulations said that first chance would be given to the residents of Alberta if they appeared in person before a branch of the treasury office, which exists in every town in Alberta, or a branch of a national bank.
I found every type of person, working people, waitresses, truck drivers, doctors, lawyers, preachers and even a few school teachers, lined up trying to get access to those shares. The figures are not precise but they are close enough. So heavy was the subscription to the shares available that they had to divide them among all the adults who appeared and each adult received a maximum of 20 shares at $5 apiece. So great was the demand by over 100,000 adult Albertan citizens that they could only give them $100 worth of shares apiece.
That is not the end of my story. I have the financial records of that company up to the last year. After years, those shares at $5 were split four ways. At one time the shares reached a peak of $45 and $50, and they were split five ways. Now they are averaging $14 and $16. So if you still have shares for $5 which you bought in 1954, and you now have four, at $16 apiece they would be worth $64. That ain't bad, Mr. Speaker. That $5 has got you $64 in 20 years. In the meantime dividends were paid and on the $16 share today the last dividend I saw was 60 cents. Sixty cents on one of your four shares is the same as $2.40 on your four shares. Any time you have a hot little share in your hand that you bought for $5, it will give you $2.40 dividend every year. That ain't bad, Mr. Speaker.
Northern Pipeline
When you take a look at the total value of the investment in the pipeline you see that large amounts went to pay the interest and pay off the capital on those orginal bonds. But who got the money? The millions of common people, each of them, got as much as 2,002 shares at $5 apiece. So if you were a big company in those days finding gas in Alberta, you probably got 50 shares at $5 apiece. Those of Class B type were multiplied by four, so there would probably be 200 shares. All the dividends they would get would be on the 200 shares.
I am simply suggesting that we should have done as the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) suggested last August when we met here and in effect approved the route. The minute the negotiations were over in the United States the government should have brought in legislation including some of these clauses and we could have had financing arranged similar to this precedent. Time has passed and I am sure these Canadian companies have gone out and arranged the financing of this pipeline with other companies. It they followed the usual precedent, with a total cost of roughly $4 billion, $1 billion will probably be the equity and $3 billion the amount of bonds.
Every one of us here, representing, as we do, every Canadian, should be asking ourselves whether these Canadian companies who are going to take the risk of backing up this equity of $1 billion will make any of these shares available to us and to every other Canadian as an individual. That is the question we should be asking. It is too late now to bring in an amendment to this bill and to get it into law, which I hope will be next month, because I am sure the financing has already been arranged.
I would like to see a monitoring committee of this House representing the people. Whether it sits every three months or two and a half weeks is immaterial, just so long as there is somebody representing the people and reminding not only the government but this company of their many promises. The company promised that if it ever got this certificate of convenience it would give Canadians a chance to invest. We want to know how the company financed the project and if it has made the shares available.
I happen to believe that the working man in Hamilton wants the extra 2 per cent or 3 per cent of business this project will bring to him next year. He is the most efficient steel producer in the world and he knows it. He can match any steelworker in the world for price per unit, and he knows that. He also knows he gets better wages than most of them too. He will accept that 2 per cent or 3 per cent of extra income in business next year.
What he would like for the next 30, 40 or 50 years, as long as gas goes through the pipeline-and whether it is U.S. gas or American gas is immaterial-is an opportunity to share in return on equity. Every time the pipeline is repaired or restored the equity life is extended. I do not think one will ever
3046

February 20, 1978
Northern Pipeline
get the amount of return one could get from the Alberta Gas Trunk because that was a brand new situation.
However, what we should be thinking about here as members of parliament is not just the failures of this government in respect of Westcoast 25 years ago, in respect of Trans-Canada Pipelines 22 years ago, or in respect of the Great Lakes application ten years ago; rather we should be thinking about all the other pipelines we are going to be building over the next ten or 20 years. These pipelines will be built not just to bring gas or oil from our remote areas, and not just to move the products of the forest in gas and oil form from east to west, west to east and north to south, but to move coal. We are going to move coal and a whole variety of products like potash in liquid form. We will have the pipelines. We have the best track record in building pipelines in the world. Above, all let us keep our eye on the ball.
The thing that gives Canadians the deepest satisfaction of all is not just the fact that Canadians own the pipeline but that Canadians get these dividend cheques every three months. One thing that the Americans have taught us is to go after the equity, because that is where you get the money. It comes in year after year after year. Just try to find on the stock markets of the United States or of Canada today any single common stock that has almost a guaranteed return of 15 per cent or more, as will be the case under this National Energy Board power to set the rate of return on the rate base. I hope it will be a lot more than 15 per cent.
In the case of Alberta Gas Trunk Line the regional guys can still get 100 per cent a year. If you get $5 a year including capital gains on a stock worth only $5, that is 100 per cent. Even if the fellow only had a couple of hundred dollars' worth, that is better than anything else he can see or buy. He will never get that again.
Maybe the next pipeline will be built as a brand new venture right here in Canada. Maybe the next time this government will be thinking of Canadians owning these things, and will have brought in changes to the capital gains tax and changes to the deferral of incomes sections of the Income Tax Act. If the government says to a man or a woman that it will defer the tax on up to $1,000 a year if they put the money into a retirement savings plan for their old age, on which the returns are pretty hairy these days, then surely it can allow the same persons to put that money into stocks in respect of which the government cam make sure they cannot lose. If that were done the workers would soon let you know where they stand. A worker knows now that on a fixed pension he is doomed when he reaches the end of his working period. He wants something indexed so it will grow with inflation; his pension will not. This is what the working man in Canada wants, and what a glorious opportunity this government had; but it failed to take advantage of it on this occasion.
I would think that if it has not learned the lessons of the last 25 years there is not much hope that this government will ever learn them. That is why I know in my heart that 50 per cent, 60 per cent or 70 per cent of the people who live in the western part of this country pray every night: "Dear God, let's get rid

of this outfit. Please God, no matter how terrible the opposition is, change the government".
Those people know that in the last 50 years the only hope they ever had was during the five years under the right hon. member for Prince Albert. They want another chance to have five, ten or 15 years of growth instead of this "stagflation". This government ran out of steam 35 years ago. It relied entirely on the mandarins of the civil service to direct it. The civil service died in 1948 and hasn't come alive since. It is still hanging on to ways of doing things that are wrong. We took the wrong fork in the road during the war years; we must have a change in government to get back on the right road so that Canadians can restore their pride in their own ability to save for their old age and, at the same time, produce the things that make this country grow and be strong.

If I am to judge from the propaganda I hear from the government side of the House, we are getting close to the end of that lifetime. Meetings have been held recently with municipal officials at which the promise was made again. Many people in the national capital region are awaiting an answer as to when this belief will be forthcoming.
Although the question was related to the national capital area, it is a national problem in that it affects every municipality in which there are formidable federal institutions. It hits Ottawa particularly hard because its major employer is the government of Canada. The federal government does not pay a business tax or anything like it. The government of Canada owns 40 per cent of the land in the area. In 1977 the Regional Municipality of Ottawa-Carleton suffered a shortfall in projected revenue of $18 million. As the cost of doing local government business increases, the burden increases.
It is not just a burden on the Regional Municipality of Ottawa-Carleton but also on people who own property and pay rent. The mayor of the city of Ottawa has estimated that the burden on his ratepayers is approximately $150 per household as a result of this. Throughout the townships of Nepean, Gloucester, Rideau and Osgoode it varies, but it approaches that figure.
This problem was brought to the attention of the Prime Minister. Two years ago he responded to it by indicating the legislation was forthcoming. When, in what form and to what extent will this relief be forthcoming? It has been promised. I hope the promise will not be recycled by announcing once again in or around April that relief is on its way. That would cause the people of Ottawa-Carleton to wonder.
The decentralization program, which is a rather perverse form of patronage, coupled with the relocation program has aggravated the situation. The Woods-Gordon report indicates a $500 million loss over the next ten years; an economic crisis which may last 15 years; $13 million in lost office revenues over the next ten years; and property value decreases, as a result of lost revenues, of approximately $30 million in that same period.
Clearly it is a serious problem for Ottawa. It means the tax base of the Ottawa-Carleton region is shrinking; the burden on the homeowner and the renter is correspondingly increasing. The federal government has promised to assist in solving the problems of the area. We would like some action on the promise which was made when relocation was announced. The federal government said it would give us assistance.
I know the parliamentary secretary is not blind, deaf or dumb. He must understand the difficulties which are faced by small business people and restaurateurs. There are problems with respect to buildings. The government of Canada pays something equivalent to property taxes. The government should finally accede to the wishes of the people and local government and bring to our area some equity to match the immense power and influence it has. For many years the government has not been paying its way completely. On behalf of ratepayers and tenants in the Ottawa area, I ask that that legislation be brought forward quickly so that the House and the public can examine it.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance intends to introduce a bill amending the Municipal Grants Act in 1978. There is no draft bill but the Department of Finance is already working hard and systematically considering the various decisions to be taken before preparing the bill itself. The Minister of Finance has asked his officials to be ready to introduce such a bill at the beginning of the session this fall. The legislation will be retroactive and enforced for the municipal taxation years from January 1, 1978.
The grant program in lieu of taxes is a national program and the amendments which will be suggested by the Minister of Finance will benefit municipalities throughout Canada, including the municipalities in the national capital area. The minister has received representations about amendments to the act from the City of Ottawa, the Federation of Canadian Municipalities and many other agencies.
All these representations are being considered. It will also be necessary to review carefully many technical problems. Everyone understands that these questions will polarize much time and resources in a year that promises to be a busy one. I can, however, assure hon. members that the schedule I have prepared will be followed. The grants in lieu of taxes program was introduced several years ago by a Liberal government and since that time more than 2,000 municipalities across the country have taken advantage of it. The new act will update the program and Canadian municipalities should welcome it.

AGRICULTURE-POTATO ACTION COMMITTEE-PROGRESS REPORT ON STUDY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 17, I asked the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) what has become of the federal-provincial committee which was responsible for setting up a marketing plan for potatoes in eastern Canada. That group is called the Potato Action Committee or PAC and that is the abbreviation I am going to use whenever I mention it. The minister told me that this committee had made recommendations but could not force the provinces to do anything. Fine, and I too agree on the principle that we should let producers organize together and decide on the best means to take to market their product in each province.
In his answer, the minister also stated that because they had refused to establish a marketing board, producers of one of the
80031-5 l'A

February 20, 1978
Adjournment Debate
provinces are now getting $2 to $3 dollar per hundredweight less than they are getting in Alberta. Without naming that province, the minister was referring of course to my province of New Brunswick. But Prince Edward Island and Ontario are in no better position.
The minister knows as well as I do that it is not the lack of a marketing board which can explain the difference in prices between New Brunswick and Alberta. Do they have a marketing board in Alberta? Unless I am mistaken, the answer is no. Moreover, the minister himself stated before the agriculture committee two years ago that a distinction had to be made between eastern and western Canada. He even went so far as to suggest that two different potato marketing boards were necessary, in order to take fully into account the particular circumstances and markets of both regions. Therefore the minister's argument is a sham. The problems and challenges involved are quite difficult and cannot be met simply by setting up marketing boards. The situation varies from one region to the next. No universal panacea exists in this area. This brings me back to the PAC which was my original concern. Last Friday, the minister did not reply to my question, and I hope his parliamentary secretary can tell us tonight whether this committee still exists, what it is doing, and whether its objectives have changed since its creation in April 1976.
One thing is sure, Mr. Speaker: The PAC will never succeed if the producers are not seriously involved in those discussions. The days when the farmers were presented with a fait accompli are a thing of the past. If they do not participate in the decisions, they will refuse to co-operate in the implementation of any proposal, no matter how good it seems to be. Should some provinces be taken to task for not having set up a potato marketing board, for having failed to find a formula that would appeal to the majority of producers? When one knows the sad story of the potato growers in New Brunswick, can the farmers be blamed for being overly careful, for not having reached a consensus? They did reach a consensus in Prince Edward Island; yet, did they get a better price for their produce this year? Not much better than in New Brunswick, and what has happened in Ontario? I shall read to the House what Farm and Country, an agricultural paper, published recently, on February 14, under the title "Potato Growers Study Board Idea", and I quote:
Both American and Prince Edward Island potatoes found their way onto the Ontario market and forced local prices below cost of production.
That is what happened, Mr. Speaker. Is that a healthy situation, when one has to sell below cost? The same newspaper also quoted Mr. Harry Fraser, editor of Fraser's Potato Newsletter of Prince Edward Island, and I quote:
New Brunswick's crop should not be a factor in the Ontario marketing decision. New Brunswick is now shut out of quality markets.
Nothing could be further from the truth, nothing could be more irresponsible. After having read that comment, I cancelled my subscription to that paper. That type of gratuitous

statement only leads to chaos. It is said, and the minister can confirm it, that Quebec and Ontario have been increasing their potato production considerably in the past few years in order to be in an excellent negotiating position if ever this happens when the quinquennial production averages will be distributed to establish provincial quotas. Where will that leave New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island whose domestic market situation is worsening year after year? If these two provinces do not have access to the central Canada market, the only solution will be processing, and here we are dealing with problems of another nature.
There is a serious problem this year, Mr. Speaker, just as there was two years ago, four years ago and so on. Cycles come back with the same frequency and potato growers disappear at the same rate. Family farms are vanishing from the picture. The point I want to make here is that marketing in itself will not settle anything. It is only an important starting point. We will have to come to an agreement in New Brunswick and elsewhere. The provinces will also have to agree among themselves, and this will not be easy. We will have to face the other problems of transportation, storage, quality of seeds, inspection, negotiations and arbitration, disease control and so on. If the PAC is always in operation, I hope it will give the leadership which is necessary to the potato industry in order to establish the consensus which all parties concerned are so eagerly seeking.
I think that the federal Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) can and should show leadership too. It will be a wasteful exercise to blame here and there or at random. Therefore, I urge the minister to stop taking shots at New Brunswick. This province is not the only one in the picture. New Brunswick probably deserves better leadership at the provincial level, and here I agree with him. What should be done is to inspire confidence, to lead the way, and New Brunswick farmers are able to carry out their responsibilities.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to answer the questions of the hon. member for Madawaska-Victoria (Mr. Corbin). And I am particularly pleased, Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that the hon. member for Madawaska-Victoria is one of those in the House who rise the most often to discuss and defend the interests of the potato producers of New Brunswick and eastern Canada. He rises because he has a good knowledge of their marketing problems and a true desire to find a solution as soon as possible, with the help of the federal Department of Agriculture.
As the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) said, the Potato Action Committee, to which I will refer as the PAC, as my colleague from Madawaska-Victoria did, made a number of recommendations and proposals regarding the establishment of potato marketing facilities for eastern Canada. The establishment of these facilities has unfortunately been delayed by its dependence on provincial authorities and by the fact that a number of producers and provinces have been unable to de-
February 20, 1978

velop appropriate organizations in their own field. Following considerable research on this subject at the producer level in the five participating provinces, the PAC got the approval of potato producers' representatives to set up a project, on July 9, 1976, in Fredericton. The essential part of this project is first to establish in each of the five provinces an agency representing the producers; second, a regional agency whose members would be delegated by the provincial organizations. The latter would be a forum and a means of coordination for regional and interprovincial aspects. It is apparent that the formation of a provincial producers' body is crucial. At the Fredericton meeting it was decided to form a producers' committee to help the PAC implement the report of the conference that took place in Montreal in 1975 and the committee at that time in fact became the proposed regional board. The board met on several occasions and is united and supported by provincial and federal officials who work in co-operation with the management of the PAC. At the beginning there was only one potato marketing agency-in Prince Edward Island. Subsequently, considerable progress was made in the development of producers' organizations. I am certain that the hon. member for Madawaska-Victoria will be as concerned as I am about the situation in New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. During the 1974-75 season those provinces received substantial financial assistance through the work of the PAC, and in New Brunswick marketing remained disorganized, as it has been for the past three years.
And it is that unfortunate fact that is the main cause of the economic problems presently facing potato producers in that province, and also the main obstacle to the PAC and the interprovincial agreement that is being sought. I must reassure the hon. member that the Potato Action Committee is very much alive and active. Its next meeting will take place on this coming March 2.

EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-ROSEAU RIVER PROJECT-VIOLATION OF BOUNDARY WATERS TREATY-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today I want to expand on the question I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) on February 14 which appears at page 2833 of Hansard. It related to questions 1 asked the minister many, many times about the position of the Canadian government with regard to the so-called Roseau River project.
The Roseau River project primarily is a channel-widening project of the Roseau River south of the forty-ninth parallel in the state of Minnesota. The purpose of that project is primarily twofold: first, to add additional land through drainage for purposes of agriculture; second, to control flooding in the state of Minnesota, especially during spring runoff.
Adjournment Debate
The effect of the Roseau River project as visualized by the U.S. army corps of engineers would have two influences on Canada which are not acceptable to Manitobans. First, the volume of flow would increase by approximately 25 per cent during peak spring runoff. We have had difficulties with flooding along the Canadian portion of the Roseau River. Second, the speed of flow would increase, especially during peak runoff periods, thus adding to erosion and to the carrying of silt along the river.
As is the procedure of the International Joint Commission, hearings were held in Manitoba in order to get the reaction of Manitobans to this project. The previous New Democratic government generally favoured the project, despite the fact that officials of the department of mines and resources and environmental management in the hearings at Dominion City on January 14, 1976 admitted under questioning that there was a possibility that article IV of the Boundary Waters Treaty could be violated if the project were to go forward as planned by the U.S. army corps of engineers.
Further, after a second study, the International Joint Commission recommended that if the project were to go ahead, the United States would be obligated to pay approximately $3.1 million in mitigating works. This figure was later increased to $4 million. This was not acceptable to Manitoba. The U.S. army corps of engineers was ready to modify the program, namely through an impoundment system whereby dams and dykes would be built and the water would be released during the low runoff period.
My question is simply this. With the change of government in Manitoba, the present Manitoba government, and I as a member of parliament throughout the years that the Roseau has been discussed, have objected to the plans because we see absolutely no benefits to Manitoba. In fact, the amount of money that would have to be paid for mitigating works simply is not sufficient, not even for the known factor projects that would have to be put into place, much less the unknown ones.
Therefore, on February 14, I specifically asked the minister what was the government of Canada's position on the Roseau River project, whether they still supported the position of the government of Manitoba, namely that the Roseau River project had no benefit to Manitoba and in fact had many detrimental effects. The minister replied at page 2833, as follows, and I think it is important to put this reply on the record:
Mr. Speaker, I would prefer to withhold the answer on that question for at least 24 hours. I had a preliminary discussion with the responsible minister from Manitoba this morning. As soon as question period is over, I will be meeting him at the Conference Centre to discuss these questions, so 1 might be in a better position to elaborate tomorrow or the next day.
I am not standing here accusing the minister for not having given me the answer. Possibly the parliamentary secretary can explain to Manitobans, specifically the constituents of Provencher and their member of parliament, the position of the government of Canada at this time. Does the government of Canada still support the position of the government of Manitoba, namely that the project should not go forward until all mitigating works are in place and are clearly understood? Are

February 20, 1978
Adjournment Debate
they also taking the position that, if these mitigating works are not regarded as adequate the recommendation should be forwarded to the International Joint Commission and to our American counterparts that the project is not acceptable? That is the issue and I await the reply of the parliamentary secretary.

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert Daudlin (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-ROSEAU RIVER PROJECT-VIOLATION OF BOUNDARY WATERS TREATY-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for having brought this question forward again so that a further answer might be provided to him.
Discussions with the United States regarding the effects on Canada of proposed flood control works along the Roseau River in Minnesota have been under way since the 1920's. An International Joint Commission report was released last fall on works planned by the U.S. corps of engineers. The report recommended that the project be allowed to go ahead, but that the United States pay $3 million to $4 million for the construction of control works in Manitoba to protect the province from possible increased flood damage. The U.S. has agreed in principle with this recommendation and has forwarded a draft agreement on the question for our examination.
The IJC was, it should be noted, requested to perform essentially an engineering study of the effects of higher flood flows. In its report, the Commission also noted, however, that
there might be other significant environmental effects above and beyond the question of flooding.
Last month, the Manitoba government indicated to the SSEA that the province had concerns over this question of unforeseen environmental effects, and that it wished to suspend further talks with the United States on Roseau until the matter had been resolved. The Canadian government is fully aware of the importance of the environmental aspects of Roseau, and has suggested that federal and provincial officials work together to clarify the matter.
We have informed United States authorities that we are currently reviewing the question of environmental effects. We have also requested further clarification of the exact form of the proposed works. The corps of engineers is currently modifying its original plans to reduce wetlands drainage, and there have been suggestions for modification of the whole concept of the scheme. The current absence of precise information on that design of the system makes it difficult for us to assess exactly the project's potential impact on Canada.
Given the forthcoming attitudes of the parties involved in the Roseau question, there is no reason to believe that a mutually satisfactory resolution cannot be achieved. We will continue to ensure that Canadian interests are fully protected.
